**Surah al-Hashr**

Al-Biqa'i said: It is also called "Surat Banu al-Nadir" (the Chapter of the Banu al-Nadir). Al-Bukhari and others related from Ibn Jubayr that he said: "I said to Ibn 'Abbas, 'Surat al-Hashr,' and he said, 'Say: Surat Banu al-Nadir.'" Ibn Hajar said: "It seems he disliked calling it 'al-Hashr' lest it be thought that the intended meaning is the Day of Resurrection, whereas what is meant here is the expulsion of the Banu al-Nadir."

It is a Medinan surah, and its verses number twenty-four without disagreement. Its connection to what precedes it: at the end of that surah is ﴿God has decreed: "I and My messengers will surely prevail"﴾ [al-Mujadila: 21], and at the beginning of this one is ﴿So God came upon them from where they did not expect, and cast terror into their hearts﴾ [al-Hashr: 2]. At the end of that surah He mentioned those who oppose God and His Messenger, and at the beginning of this one He mentioned those who defy God and His Messenger. In the first surah He mentioned the condition of the hypocrites and the Jews and the allegiance of some of them to others, and in this one He mentioned what befell the Jews and that the allegiance of the hypocrites to them did not avail them anything.

It is related that the Banu al-Nadir had made a treaty with the Messenger of God (ﷺ) that they would neither be against him nor with him. When he prevailed at the Battle of Badr, they said: "He is the Prophet described in the Torah, whose banner will never be turned back." But when the Muslims were defeated at the Battle of Uhud, they doubted and broke the treaty. Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf set out with forty riders to Mecca, and they formed an alliance with the Quraysh at the Ka'bah. Jibril, peace be upon him, informed the Messenger of God (ﷺ) of this, and he ordered the killing of Ka'b. Muhammad ibn Maslamah killed him by stealth while he was a newlywed, after his foster-brother Abu Na'ilah Silkan ibn Salamah, one of the Banu 'Abd al-Ashhal, had seized the hair at the back of his head. The Prophet (ﷺ) had also become aware of their treachery when he went to them seeking their help regarding the blood-money (diyah) of the Muslims, the two men from the Banu 'Amir whom 'Amr ibn Umayyah al-Damri had killed on his way back from the well of Ma'unah. They intended to drop a stone on the Prophet (ﷺ), but God protected him.

A few months after Ka'b was killed, according to the sound view and not according to the report that is cited, the Prophet (ﷺ) ordered preparations for war against them and for marching towards them. This was in the fourth year (AH), in the month of Rabi' al-Awwal. They were in a village called al-Zuhrah. The Muslims marched with him (ﷺ), and he was riding a donkey with a halter of palm fiber. It is said he was riding a camel. He appointed Ibn Umm Maktum as his deputy over Medina. When he (ﷺ) arrived with them, he found them wailing over Ka'b, and they said: "Leave us to weep for our noble ones; then decide your matter." He said: "Leave Medina." They said: "Death is nearer to us than that." Then they called out for war. It is also said that they asked him for a delay of ten days so that they could prepare to depart. The hypocrites, 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy and his like, sent word to them not to leave the fortress: "If they fight you, we will be with you and will surely support you, and if you are expelled, we will surely leave with you." So they fortified the alleys and reinforced them. Then they agreed to betray the Messenger of God (ﷺ). They said: "Come out with thirty of your companions, and thirty of ours will come out so that they may listen to you. If they believe you, we will all believe." He did so. They said: "How can we understand while we are sixty? Come out with three, and three of our scholars will come out to you." He (ﷺ) did so. They then concealed daggers and intended to assassinate him. A woman among them sent a sincere message to her brother, who was a Muslim, informing him of what they intended. He hastened to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and told him secretly of their plan before they could reach him.

The next day he (ﷺ) went out against them with the battalions and besieged them, according to what Ibn Hisham said in his Sirah, for six nights. It is said for twenty-one nights. Then God cast terror into their hearts, and they despaired of the support of the hypocrites, so they sought reconciliation. The Prophet (ﷺ) refused to accept anything from them except expulsion, on condition that each three of them could carry on a camel as many of their goods as they wished. They went to Syria, to Jericho and Adhri'at, except for two households of them: the family of Salam ibn Abi al-Huqayq, the family of Kinanah ibn al-Rabi' ibn Abi al-Huqayq, and the family of Huyayy ibn Akhtab. They joined Khaybar. A group joined al-Hirah. The Prophet (ﷺ) took their property and weapons. He found fifty coats of mail, fifty helmets, and three hundred and forty swords. Ibn Ubayy had told them: "I have two thousand men from my people and others, who will support you, and Qurayzah and your allies from Ghatafan will support you." When the Prophet (ﷺ) besieged them, Qurayzah withdrew from them, Ibn Ubayy abandoned them, and so did their allies from Ghatafan. Then God revealed His saying, Mighty and Majestic:

[Page 39]

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. ﴿Whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth glorifies God, and He is the Mighty, the Wise﴾ up to His saying, ﴿And God is over all things competent﴾ [al-Hashr: 6]. The discussion of the like of this sentence has already passed at the beginning of Surat al-Hadid. Here He repeated the relative pronoun for the increase of affirmation and to draw attention to the independence of each of the two groups in glorifying God,

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 59, verse 2 (part 1 of 2):

The saying of Allah, Exalted is He: ﴿It is He who expelled those who disbelieved among the People of the Book from their homes﴾ is an explanation of some of the effects of His might (ʿizzah) and the judgements of His wisdom (ḥikmah), following His description, Exalted is He, with overwhelming might and dazzling wisdom absolutely. By "those who disbelieved" is meant the Banu al-Nadir (bani al-Nadir, on the pattern of al-Amir), who were a great tribe of the Jews of Khaybar, like the Banu Qurayzah. The two tribes are also called "al-Kahinan" (the two priests), because they are from the progeny of the priest Ibn Harun, as mentioned in al-Bahr. It is also said that they settled near Madinah, in a group of the Children of Israel, awaiting the coming out of the Messenger (ﷺ), and what happened to them was what Allah, Exalted is He, related.

It has been said that Musa (ʿalayhi al-salam) had sent them to kill the Amalekites, and said to them: "Do not spare any of them." They went but did not do it, and disobeyed Musa (ʿalayhi al-salam). When they returned to al-Sham, they found that he (ʿalayhi al-salam) had died. The Children of Israel said to them: "You are disobedient to Allah, Exalted is He; by Allah, you shall not enter our lands upon us." So they withdrew to the Hijaz, until what happened happened. It is narrated from al-Hasan that they were the Banu Qurayzah, but this is an error, as is not hidden. The first preposition phrase ("min ahl al-kitab") is attached to an omitted verb, meaning "being from the People of the Book," and the second is attached to "akhraja." The attribution of the homes (diyar) to them is valid, because they had settled in an open desert with no settlement, so they built in it and dwelt there. The pronoun "huwa" refers to Him, Exalted is He, under the title of might and wisdom, either based on the complete manifestation of His attributes of these two qualities together with full assistance from the context, or by treating it as a substitute for the demonstrative, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Say: Have you considered, if Allah took your hearing and your sight and sealed over your hearts, who is a god other than Allah to bring them to you?﴾ [al-An'am: 46], meaning "by that." It is as if it were said: "That One described with might and wisdom who expelled..." etc. In this there is a hint that in the expulsion there is dazzling wisdom. His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿at the first gathering﴾ is attached to "akhraja," and the lam is the lam of time, like the one in their saying: "I wrote it for ten nights past." Its ultimate meaning returns to the sense of "in" (fi) of place/time. That is why they said here, i.e. "in the first gathering," but they did not say that it has the meaning of "in," to indicate that it has not departed from its original meaning, and that it is for specification, because what occurred in a time is specified to it apart from other times. It has been said that it is for causation, but this is not right. The meaning of "awwal al-hashr" is that this is the first of their gatherings to al-Sham, i.e. the first time they were gathered and expelled. By mentioning the firstness, it is indicated that they had not been subjected to exile before, and Bukhtnassar did not exile them when he exiled the Jews, based on the view that they were not with them at that time, and that their transfer from the lands of al-Sham to the land of the Arabs was by their own choice; or that this did not befall them in Islam; or that they are the first of the People of the Book gathered from the Arabian Peninsula to al-Sham. In this, no consideration is given to contrasting the first with the last. Some take it as contrasting, so the meaning of "awwal al-hashr" is that this is the first of their gatherings and the last of their gatherings was the expulsion of ʿUmar (raḍiya Allahu ʿanhu) of them from Khaybar to al-Sham. It has been said: the last of their gatherings will be their gathering on the Day of Resurrection, because the place of gathering will be in al-Sham.

From ʿIkrimah: "Whoever doubts that the place of gathering here means al-Sham, let him recite this verse." It seems he derived this from the fact that the first meaning is their gathering to al-Sham, so that they would have a last gathering to it as well, for the contrast to be complete, namely the Day of Resurrection from the graves. It is not hidden that this is weak in its indication. In al-Bahr, from ʿIkrimah and al-Zuhri, that both said: the meaning is "for the first subject of gathering," which is al-Sham. In a hadith, the Prophet (ﷺ) said to them: "Go out." They said: "To where?" He said: "To the land of the gathering." The weakness of this meaning is also not hidden. It has been said: the last of their gatherings is that a fire will come out before the Hour and gather them as it gathers the rest of people from east to west. From al-Hasan: it was intended the gathering of Resurrection, i.e. this is its first part and the rising from the graves is its last, and this is as you see. It has been said: the meaning is that He expelled them from their homes for the first assembly that the Prophet (ﷺ) gathered, or that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, gathered for fighting them, because the Prophet (ﷺ) had not previously intended to fight them. In this there is suitability to the description of might that is not hidden, and for this reason it has been said that this is the apparent meaning. It was objected that the Prophet (ﷺ) had not gathered the Muslims to fight them on this occasion either, and therefore he (ﷺ) rode a donkey with a halter of palm fiber, out of indifference to them. This is open to question. It has been said: it is for the first gathering of them for fighting from among the Muslims, because they had not gathered for it before. "Hashr" is the expulsion of a group, whether of people for war or not. Yes, it is conditioned that the one gathered be a group of living beings only. The legitimacy of expulsion (ijla') was at the beginning of Islam, but now it has been abrogated (nusikhat), and only killing, enslavement, or imposing the jizya is permitted. ﴿You did not think﴾, O Muslims, ﴿that they would go out﴾, because of the severity of their might, the strength of their defences, the firmness of their fortresses, and the abundance of their number and equipment.

﴿And they thought that their fortresses would protect them from Allah﴾, i.e. they thought that their fortresses would prevent them, or protect them from the might of Allah, Exalted is He. "Husunuhum" is the subject, and "mani'atuhum" is the predicate placed first, and the clause is the predicate of "anna." The apparent wording, to match "ma zanantum an yakhrujū," would have been "wa-zannū an lā yakhrujū," but the shift to what is in the sublime wording indicates the difference between the two suppositions, and that their supposition approached certainty, so it was fitting to use what indicates their extreme confidence in their condition. Thus "mani'atuhum" is used, with "ḥuṣūnuhum" following, placing the predicate before the subject; the basis of the indication is the fronting, because of the exclusivity it carries, as if there were no fortress more protective than their fortresses. And with what indicates their belief within themselves that they were in might and protection, with which they cared for no one who would attack them or seek their weakness, the pronoun "hum" is brought and made the subject of "anna," and it is predicated by the clause, because of what this contains of the sense of strengthening (al-taqwa), according to al-Kashshaf and the Sharh of al-Tibi. Whether that is of the type of strengthening is open to discussion. Some prevented the permissibility of the previous parsing, on the basis that fronting a derived predicate before a subject that could be a subject is not permitted, like fronting a verbal predicate. They permitted it for the derived (participle) but not the verb. Yes, the author of al-Fara'id preferred that "ḥuṣūnuhum" be the subject of "māni'atuhum," because it depends on the subject.

It was also allowed that "māni'atuhum" be a subject with predicate "ḥuṣūnuhum." It was objected that this involves predicating an indefinite noun by a definite one if the construction is a verbal (lafẓī) one that is preventing, and that the meaning would not be so if it were a semantic (ma'nawī) construction, by intending the continuation of prevention; so reflect. "Ḥuṣūnuhum" was, as it is said, four: al-Katība, al-Waṭīḥ, al-Salālim, and al-Naṭāh. Some added al-Wakhda, and some Shiqq. What is in the Qamus is that it is a place in Khaybar or a valley in it.

﴿Then Allah came upon them﴾, i.e. His command, Exalted is He, and His decree, Mighty and Majestic, which was determined for them ﴿from where they did not reckon﴾ and did not occur to their minds. It is, as narrated from al-Suddi, Abu Salih, and Ibn Jurayj, the killing of their chief Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf, for this was among what weakened their strength, diminished their power, and stripped their hearts of security and tranquility. It has been said: the pronoun in "fa-atahum" and "lam yahtasibu" refers to the believers, i.e. the help of Allah came to them from where they did not reckon; and in this is a dislocation of pronouns.

It was read "fa-ataahum Allah," and then it is transitive to two objects, the second of which is omitted, i.e. "Allah gave them the punishment or the victory." ﴿And He cast terror into their hearts﴾, i.e. intense fear, from "raʿabtu al-ḥawḍ" (I filled the basin), because it is imagined that it filled the heart. The original meaning of "qadhf" is throwing with force or from a distance, and what is meant here by convention is the establishment of that and its implanting in their hearts.

﴿They destroyed their houses with their own hands﴾, so that with what they dismantled of them of wood and stones they might block the openings of the alleys, and so that they would not remain fit for habitation by the Muslims after their exile, and so that they might take away some of their desirable fittings that can be moved, such as wood, pillars and doors. ﴿And the hands of the believers﴾, where they destroyed them from outside so that they could enter upon them, remove their fortification, and widen the field of battle, and so that their harm would increase. Since the destruction by the hands of the believers was caused by the command of those Jews, the destruction by the hands of the believers is as if it proceeded from them, and on this basis "the hands of the believers" is conjoined to "their hands" and made an instrument of their destruction, even though the instrument is their own hands. Thus "fa-yukhribūna" according to this is either from combining the literal and the metaphorical, or from the generality of metaphor. The clause is either in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in "qulubihim," or it has no place in the grammatical structure. It is either a resumptive answer to a question assumed to be: "What was their condition after the terror?" or "with it," or an explanation of the terror by claiming unity, because what they did indicates their terror, for had it not been so, they would not have destroyed them.

Qatadah, al-Jahdari, Mujahid, Abu Haywah, ʿIsa and Abu ʿAmr read "yukhattibūna" with doubling, and it is for intensification in the act or in the object; it was allowed that it be in the agent. Abu ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAla said: kharraba means demolished and ruined, and akhraba means left the place in ruin and went away from it, so ikhrab is the effect of takhrib. It has been said: both have the same meaning, the intransitive "khariba" being made transitive by doubling at one time and by the hamza at another.

﴿So take warning, O people of insight﴾, i.e. learn a lesson from what befell them of the great matters, in a manner that thought can hardly reach; beware of engaging in what led them to disbelief and sins; and pass over from their state, in their treachery and their reliance on other than Allah, Exalted is He, which became the cause of the destruction of their houses by their own hands and the hands of their enemies, and of their departure from their homelands compelled, to the state of your own selves. So do not rely on the convergence of causes, and do not depend on other than Him, Mighty and Majestic; rather, put your trust in Him, Exalted is He.

The argument from this verse for the legitimacy of acting upon legal analogy (qiyas al-shar'i) is well known. They said: He, Exalted is He, commanded in it "i'tibar," which is passing over and moving from one thing to another, and that is realized in analogy, since in it the ruling is transferred from the source (asl) to the branch (far'). For this reason Ibn ʿAbbas said concerning teeth: he drew an analogy of their ruling from fingers, in that their blood-money is equal. The basic principle in unrestricted usage is the literal meaning. Since the command is established, and it is apparent in a demand not departing from the requirement of obligation or recommendation, the legitimacy of acting on analogy is established. It was objected, after granting that the command is apparent in demand, that we do not grant that "i'tibar" means what was mentioned; rather it is an expression for "being admonished," since that is what is understood when it is used unqualified, and the arrangement of it with "fa" after what precedes it in the verse indicates this, as in His saying, Exalted is He: "Indeed in that is a lesson for people of insight" [Al ʿImran: 13; al-Nur: 44], and ﴿Indeed in the cattle is a lesson for you﴾ [al-Nahl: 66]. Also, when a person who analogizes engages in sins and does not reflect on the matter of his afterlife, it is said that he is not one who takes heed, and had analogy been i'tibar, this negation would not be valid. Granting that, still there is in the verse no general wording that requires acting upon every analogy; rather it is unrestricted, so acting on it is satisfied by acting on rational analogy. Granting that, the general term is nonetheless specified by consensus, since you have said: if someone tells his agent, "Free Ghanim because he is black," it is not permitted for that to extend to Salim even if he is black.

So far as the restriction goes, it does not remain a proof for anything beyond the locus of the restriction. Granting, however, that the address is to those present at the time, it is confined to them. It has been answered: if "i'tibar" in its unrestricted sense meant admonition (ittiʿaz), then the statement "i'tabara fa-ittaʿaza" ("he took heed and was admonished") would not be well-formed, because it would then imply a thing being consequent upon itself. Its placement in the verse after what precedes it does not prevent it from meaning the transition mentioned, because that transition is realized in admonition: the one admonished by another moves from knowledge of the state of that other to knowledge of the state of himself. Thus he is commanded to do it by virtue of the transition involved in it, which is analogy (qiyas). The two verses are to be understood accordingly. It is not valid that the sinning analogist be excluded from the meaning, in view of his being an analogist; rather it is valid in view of the matter of the Hereafter. The negation is stated absolutely because it concerns the greatest of aims, and he has neglected it. If the verse indicates generality, that is well; if it indicates only the unrestricted sense, it is necessary to interpret it as referring to the legal analogy (al-qiyas al-shar'i), because the Lawgiver usually addresses us with legal matters rather than others. It has been demonstrated that the general term after restriction is a proof, and the extension of the ruling of an address to those present to others until the Day of Resurrection has been established by consensus (ijma'). The disagreement over whether the wording extends or not does no harm; moreover, whether it is general or not, it is a proof against the opponents regarding part of the locus of dispute, and from this the ruling on the remainder necessarily follows, since no one holds a distinction.

Al-Khafaji said, regarding the mode of inference: They said: we are commanded in this verse to i'tibar, which is returning a thing to its counterpart by ruling on it with the ruling of that counterpart. This includes admonition, rational analogy, and legal analogy. The context of the verse is admonition, so it indicates that by its explicit expression (ʿibarah), and it indicates analogy by allusion (ishara). The full discussion of this is in the books of usul al-fiqh.

﴿Had it not been that God had decreed for them the exile﴾, that is, the expulsion or the departure from their homelands in that dreadful manner, ﴿He would have punished them in this world﴾ by killing, as He did with the people of Badr and others, or as He did with the Banu Qurayza in the fifth year. Wisdom requires this if exile had not been decreed for them. It is said: "Ajlaytu al-qawma 'an manazilihim" (I caused the people to leave their dwellings), meaning I expelled them from them and drove them out into the open, and "jalaw 'anha" (they departed from it), meaning they went out or came out into the open. It is also said: "jalahum" (he exiled them). Some scholars distinguish between *al-jalaʾ* and *al-ikhraj* (expulsion): *al-jalaʾ* is when it occurs together with the family and children, whereas *al-ikhraj* may occur while the family and children remain.

Al-Mawardi said: *al-jalaʾ* occurs only to a group, whereas *al-ikhraj* may occur to an individual or to a group. It is also said *al-jalaʾ*, with a hamza and without an alif, like *al-naba'* (the news). Al-Hasan ibn Salih, his brother Ali ibn Salih, and Talha recited it this way. The word *an* (that) is a verbal (*masdariyyah*) particle, not a light (*mukhaffafah*) form whose noun is a pronoun of the matter, as the wording of al-Kashshaf may suggest; al-Radi has explicitly stated this.

God's words ﴿And for them in the Hereafter is the punishment of the Fire﴾ form a resumed statement (*istinaf*) not connected to the answer of *law-la* (had it not been). That is: if they escape the punishment of this world, which is killing, by means of a matter more grievous for them, which is exile, they have not escaped the punishment of the Hereafter. Thus their enjoyment of a few days of life, and their making light of the matter of exile for their own souls, does them no good. This implies that killing is more severe than exile, not in itself, but because through it they reach the punishment of the Fire. Exile was chosen because it is more difficult for them, and because they either do not believe in what lies before them of the punishment of the Fire, or they believe in it but do not care for it at all. It was not made a circumstantial clause (*hal*), because that would require interpretation due to the lack of simultaneity.

﴿That﴾ means what befell them and what will befall them, ﴿because﴾ of the cause that ﴿they opposed Allah and His Messenger﴾, and committed what they committed of foul deeds. ﴿And whoever opposes Allah﴾. Talha read ﴿yushaqiq﴾ (يُشاقِقْ) with ﻿*fakk* (the separation of the two identical consonants, as in al-Anfal). Restricting the mention to opposing Him, glorified and exalted is He, is because opposing Him includes opposing him, upon him be prayers and peace (ﷺ). In it there is also what there is of magnifying the gravity of the matter, and it accords with His saying, exalted is He: ﴿for indeed Allah is severe in punishment﴾.

This sentence is either the apodosis (*al-jaza'*, the consequent of the conditional) itself, in which case the returning pronoun (*al-'a'id*, the pronoun linking it back to the antecedent) has been omitted from it according to those who require it, meaning "severe in punishment for him"; or it is a justification (*ta'lil*) for the omitted apodosis, meaning "Allah will punish him, for indeed Allah is severe in punishment." In either case, the conditional clause (*al-shartiyyah*, the conditional sentence) completes what precedes it, confirms its meaning, and establishes the causal link through a demonstrative method, as if it were said: "That punishment which has befallen them and will befall them is because of their opposing Allah, exalted is He, and His Messenger, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him (ﷺ). Whoever opposes Allah, exalted is He, whoever he may be, will for that reason receive a severe punishment. So for them there is a severe punishment."

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 59, verse 5:

﴿Whatever palm trees (linah) you cut down﴾: it refers to the palm tree in general, according to what al-Hasan, Mujahid, Ibn Zayd, 'Amr ibn Maymun and al-Raghib said. It is of the form fi'lah from the root "lawn" (color), and its ya' is converted from a waw because of the kasra before it, as in diyma (a steady rain). Its plural is alwan (colors). Ibn 'Abbas and a group of the people of language said: it is the palm tree that is not 'ajwa (a type of date). Abu 'Ubayda and Sufyan said: its dates are lawana, which is a kind of date. Sufyan said: it is very yellow, its pit showing through so that it is seen from the outside. Abu 'Ubayda also said: it is the mixed varieties of palm trees among which there is neither 'ajwa nor barni. Ja'far al-Sadiq, may Allah be pleased with him, said: it is the 'ajwa. Al-Asma'i said: it is the daqal (a poor-quality date). It was also said: it is the short palm tree. Al-Thawri said: it is the noble palm tree, as if they derived it from linah (softness), so its plural is liyan. Its plural came as liyan, as in the words of Imru' al-Qays:

"And a long neck like the markets of the liyan, in which the strong torch kindled its flame."

It was also said: it refers to the branches of trees because of their softness, but this is an anomalous view. They cited, to support its meaning of the palm tree, whether it derives from color or from softness, the words of Dhu al-Rummah:

"As if above them (my saddle-frame) is a bird's nest, upon a straight-trunked linah whose sides flutter."

It is possible to say: he meant by linah the noble palm tree, because he describes the she-camel as being of noble lineage in generosity, so the comparison should point to that meaning. What follows "ma" is a conditional particle in the accusative case, governed by "qata'tum", and "min linatin" is its explanation. For this reason the pronoun in His words, exalted is He, ﴿or you left them standing on their roots﴾ is feminine: that is, you left them as they were and did not touch them in any way. The answer of the conditional is His words, glorified is He, ﴿then it was by the permission of Allah﴾: that is, that cutting them or leaving them was by the command of Allah, exalted, which reached you through His Messenger ﷺ, or by His will and His pleasure, mighty and majestic.

Abdullah, al-A'mash and Zayd ibn 'Ali read qawman (قَوْمًا) on the pattern fa'l, like darb, as the plural of qa'im. It was also read qa'iman (قائِمًا), a masculine active participle agreeing with the wording of ma, and they kept usulaha (أُصُولَها) in the feminine. It was also read asluha (أصْلُها) with two dammas. Its original form is usulaha, and the waw was deleted, being sufficient with the damma; or it is kurhun with two dammas without deletion and lightening.

﴿And that He might disgrace the defiantly disobedient﴾: it is connected to an implied element, on the basis that it is a cause for that element, and that implied element is joined to another implied element, meaning: that He might honor the believers and that He might disgrace the defiantly disobedient, that is, to humiliate them. Allah, mighty and majestic, permitted the cutting and the leaving. It is also permitted that it be joined to His words, ﴿by the permission of Allah﴾, and the cause is joined to the means, so there is no need for an implied element there. By "the defiantly disobedient" is meant those among the People of the Book who disbelieved. The apparent noun was placed in the position of the pronoun to indicate the reason for the ruling. The consideration of cutting and leaving in the caused element is the apparent one. Their humiliation by cutting the palm trees is due to their grief at its loss at the hands of their Muslim enemies, and by leaving them is due to their grief at its remaining in the hands of those enemies. Thus in al-Intisaf.

Some said: These two griefs are realized whatever was cut or left, because palm trees in general are dear to their owners, so their souls hardly allow their enemies to dispose of them as they wish, and their dearness to the one who planted them is greater than their dearness to someone other than the planter. I have heard some planters say: "The frond is to me like a finger of my hand." The realization of grief at the loss is clearer if the cut tree was the noble palm, and likewise its realization at its remaining in the hands of their Muslim enemies if it was the one left standing. What some reports indicate is that some of the Companions used to cut the noble palms and others cut other kinds, and the Prophet ﷺ approved both: the first when he made clear that his aim was to enrage the disbelievers, and the second when he said that it was to preserve the noble palms for the Muslims. This was the first occasion on which the Muslims descended upon those disbelievers and besieged them. It is narrated that at the outset of the war he, upon whom be prayers and peace, ordered the cutting of their palm trees. They said: "O Muhammad, you used to forbid corruption on the earth, so what is the matter with cutting and burning the palm trees?" Then the verse was revealed: ﴿Whatever palm trees you cut down﴾, and so on. It did not explicitly mention burning, because it is in the meaning of cutting, so it sufficed with that. As for mentioning leaving, although it is not corruption in their view either, it is to establish that cutting is not corruption, placing it in the same line as what is not corruption, as a notice that the two are equal in that respect.

The verse has been cited as evidence for the permissibility of demolishing the dwellings of disbelievers, cutting their trees, and burning their crops in order to enrage them. The summary of what the jurists have said on this question is that if it is known that those things will remain in the hands of the disbelievers, then destruction and burning are preferable; otherwise, leaving them is preferable, unless that involves a benefit,

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 59, verse 6:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And what Allah restored to His Messenger from them﴾ begins an explanation of the condition of what was taken from their wealth, after explaining what befell them of the immediate and deferred punishment, and what was done to their homes and palm trees of destruction and cutting down. That is, what Allah the Exalted returned to His Messenger ﷺ from those disbelievers, who are the Banu al-Nadir. "Ma" (what) is a relative pronoun serving as the subject (mubtada'), the sentence after it is its relative clause (silah), and the returning pronoun (al-'a'id) is omitted, as we have indicated. The sentence introduced by the fa' (fa-) after it is the predicate (khabar). It is permissible for it to be a conditional (shartiyyah), in which case the sentence following it is the response (jawab). What is meant by what He, glorified is He, restored to him, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, from them, is their wealth that remained after their expulsion. What is meant by its "restoration" to him, peace be upon him, is its transfer to him. This, if it does not require that it had previously been in his possession, is analogous to what has been said regarding His saying, exalted is He: "or you will return to our religion" [al-A'raf: 88; Ibrahim: 13], and is apparent; but if it requires that it had previously been in his possession, then in what has been mentioned it is a metaphor. In it there is an indication that it was fitting for it to belong to him, ﷺ, and that it had fallen into their hands without right, so Allah the Exalted returned it to its rightful owner. The same applies to all the wealth of the disbelievers which becomes fay' for the believers, because Allah, mighty and majestic, created people for His worship, and created whatever He created of wealth so that they might use it as a means to His obedience; so it is worthy that it belong to the obedient. For this reason, the spoils that involve no hardship are called fay', even though it derives from fa'a al-zill (the shade returned) when it returns. Al-Raghib related from some of them that it was named thus by way of likening it to the fay' which is the shade, as an alert that the most noble of the worldly goods passes like a fleeting shadow. And "afa'a" with respect to what is in al-Bahr means the present tense. As for when "ma" is conditional, this is evident; and as for when it is relative, it is because when the fa' is in its predicate, it is considered similar to the conditional noun. If the verse was revealed before their expulsion, it would be informing of the unseen; and if it was revealed after their expulsion and the arrival of their wealth in the hand of the Messenger ﷺ, it would be an explanation of what is future, and the ruling of the past is the ruling of it. What the reports indicate is that it was revealed afterwards. It is narrated that when the Banu al-Nadir were expelled from their homelands and left their houses and wealth, the Muslims requested that it be divided into fifths like the spoils of Badr, and so there was revealed: ﴿And what Allah restored to His Messenger from them, you did not make any expedition for it﴾, etc., and it became exclusively for the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. Al-Bukhari, Muslim, Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i and others have related from Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: The wealth of the Banu al-Nadir was among what Allah the Exalted restored to His Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, of what the Muslims had not pressed toward with horses or riding camels, and it was exclusively for the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. He would spend from it on his family the provision of a year, and then he would place what remained in weapons and horses as a reserve in the way of Allah the Exalted.

Al-Dahhak said: It was exclusively his, ﷺ, so he gave preference to the Muhajirun with it and distributed it among them, and he did not give the Ansar any of it except Abu Dujanah Simak ibn Kharashah, Sahl ibn Hunayf and al-Harith ibn al-Simmah, whom he gave because of their poverty. Ibn Hisham mentioned something similar, except that he mentioned the first two and did not mention al-Harith; likewise Ibn Sayyid al-Nas did not mention him, and he mentioned that he gave Sa'd ibn Mu'adh a sword of Ibn Abi al-Haqiq, which had a reputation among them. The meaning of "ma awjftum 'alayhi" (what you pressed toward for it) is what you caused to be driven in obtaining it, from al-wajif, which is rapidity of travel. Abu Hayyan cited as evidence the verse of Nusayb:

Ala rubba rakbin qad qata'ta wajifahum ilayka wa-lawla anta lam tuwjifa al-rakbu
And Ibn Hisham said: "awjftum" means you moved and wearied yourselves in traveling, and he cited the verse of Tamim ibn Muqbil:

Madhawid bil-bid al-hadith suqaluha ∗∗∗ 'an al-rakbi ahyanan idha al-rakbu awjafu
The outcome is one. The "min" in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿of horses﴾ is extra, in the object, for the sake of specifying generality, as if it were said: "what you pressed toward for it" — not a single individual of horses at all — ﴿nor riding camels﴾, nor what is ridden of camels, which is predominated, just as the rider is predominated over his mount; so one does not say, in the more eloquent usage, "rakib" for one who is on a horse or donkey or the like, but rather "faris" and the like, even though that is general in meaning by its lexical imposition. They did not make use of horses or riding camels, but rather they walked to the fortresses of the Banu al-Nadir on foot, except the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, for he was on a donkey, or on a camel, as has passed, because they were close, about two miles from Medina, so they were very near to it. The intent is that what was obtained was not obtained with hardship upon you nor with fighting worth counting from you. For this reason the Messenger of Allah ﷺ did not give the Ansar except those you have heard of. As for his giving to the Muhajirun, perhaps it was because they were strangers, so their strangeness was treated as the state of travel and jihad. When it was indicated that this acquisition was not by their deeds, it was indicated what caused it by His saying, mighty and majestic: ﴿But Allah gives His messengers power over whomever He wills﴾, i.e., but His custom, mighty and majestic, operates by giving His messengers power over whomever He wills of their enemies, a particular empowerment. He empowered His messenger Muhammad ﷺ over these with an empowerment not customary, without your plunging into the narrow straits of calamities or enduring the severe hardships of wars. So you have no right to their wealth, and its matter is entrusted to him, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. ﴿And Allah is over all things Competent﴾, so He does what He wills as He wills, at times in the known manners, and at others in other manners. It has been said that the verse concerns Fadak, because the Banu al-Nadir were besieged and fought against, unlike the people of Fadak; but this contradicts what the reports have authentically established, and the fighting that occurred was something not worth counting.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 59, verse 7 (part 1 of 2):**

﴿Whatever Allah has granted as fay' (spoils gained without battle) to His Messenger from the people of the towns, it belongs to Allah and to the Messenger, and to the near of kin, the orphans, the needy, and the wayfarer.﴾ This explains the ruling on what Allah, exalted is He, granted to His Messenger ﷺ from the towns of the disbelievers, in general terms, after the ruling on what He granted him from the Banu al-Nadir had been explained. This is as Qadi Abu Yusuf related in *Kitab al-Kharaj* from Muhammad ibn Ishaq, from al-Zuhri, from Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him. His statement, may Allah be pleased with him, in a long hadith that contains the dispute between Ali, may Allah honor his face, and al-Abbas over the matter of Fadak, also indicates this. It was recorded by al-Bukhari, Muslim, Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i, and others. Thus the sentence is an answer to an implied question arising from what was understood from the preceding discourse. It is as if someone were saying: "We have known the ruling on what Allah granted from the Banu al-Nadir; so what is the ruling on what He, mighty and majestic, granted from other than them?" The answer is: "Whatever Allah granted to His Messenger from the people of the towns," and so on. For this reason it was not conjoined to what preceded it. The verse does not mention the qualifier of *iyjaf* (urging on by horse and camel, i.e., fighting) or its absence. What is understood from the books of some Shafi'is is that what this verse includes is the ruling of *fay'*, not *ghanimah* (spoils of war), nor the more general category. They distinguished between the two, saying: *Fay'* is what is obtained from the disbelievers without fighting and without urging on horses and camels, such as the poll-tax (*jizyah*) and the tithe on trade, and what they are reconciled upon without fighting of any kind, and what they abandon out of fear before the two armies meet. After the meeting of the two armies, it is *ghanimah*. [*Fay'* also includes] what belongs to an apostate who was killed or died in his apostasy, and to a dhimmi, a mu'ahad (one under treaty), or a musta'man (one under safe-conduct) who died without a heir who exhausts the estate. *Ghanimah* is what is obtained from original, belligerent disbelievers by fighting; and its ruling includes the meeting of the two armies, or our urging on [of horses and camels], not that of dhimmis, for that is theirs and is not subject to the *khums* (one-fifth). Its ruling is well known.

Also, more than one of our (Shafi'i) companions explicitly stated this distinction, citing *al-Maghrib* and others. They said: *Ghanimah* is what is taken from the disbelievers by force while the war is ongoing, and its ruling is that one-fifth of it is set aside, and the remainder belongs to the fighters alone. *Fay'* is what is taken from them after the war has laid down its burdens and the land has become a land of Islam. Its ruling is that it belongs to all Muslims and is not subject to the *khums*, meaning that all of it is spent on their public interests. Ibn Hajar transmitted this ruling from the other three imams besides al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him. The *khums* (division into fifths) on his view is based on analogy with the *ghanimah* that is divided into fifths by explicit text, with the common cause that both come to us from the disbelievers. The difference in the cause, whether fighting or its absence, has no effect. What the sound reports have stated is that Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, did with the land of Sawad in Iraq what the verse includes. He regarded it as belonging to all Muslims, citing the verse against al-Zubayr, Bilal, Salman al-Farisi, and others when they asked him to divide it among the fighters, with its estates and its non-Arab cultivators. Ali, Uthman, Talhah, and most of the others agreed with him in what he intended, even the dissenters, after he had said, addressing [Bilal]: "O Allah, suffice me against Bilal and his companions." Yet the well-known position in the books of the military campaigns is that Sawad was conquered by force, and this would imply that it was *ghanimah* and should be divided among the fighters. That is why some Shafi'is said: Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, pleased the hearts of the fighters until they gave up their right, and then he restored Sawad to its people in exchange for a *kharaj* (land tax) which they would pay every year. So let this be examined and verified.

As for what Allah, exalted is He, appointed from it to those included in His words, ﴿so it belongs to Allah and to the Messenger﴾ up to "the wayfarer" — it is the *khums* of *fay'*, as some Shafi'is explicitly stated. This *khums* is divided into five shares: for those whom Allah, mighty and majestic, mentioned. His share, glory be to Him, and the share of His Messenger, are one. His mention, exalted is He, as related from Ibn Abbas and al-Hasan ibn Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyyah, is an opening of speech for blessing and sanctification, for to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. It also contains the exaltation of the status of the Messenger, upon him be blessings and peace.

Abu al-Aliyah said: Allah's share is fixed and is to be spent on the building of His House, which is the honored Ka'bah, if it is near; otherwise, on the mosque of every town in which the *khums* is established. This implies that the shares would be six, which contradicts what is known from the early generation (*salaf*) regarding the interpretation of this. The share of the Messenger, upon him be blessings and peace, was his during his lifetime by consensus. It was one-fifth of the *khums*. He would spend from it on himself and his dependents, and would save from it his provision for a year, that is, for some of his wives, and he would spend the remainder on the public interests of the Muslims. With us, after his death, upon him be blessings and peace, it lapsed. They said: This is because the practice of the rightly-guided caliphs was upon that, and they are the trustees of Allah over His religion; and because the ruling is linked to a derived attribute, namely "the Messenger," so the root of the derivation, namely "the message," is the effective cause, and it was not found in anyone after him. This is like the lapsing of the *safi* (the chosen portion taken by the leader).

It is reported from al-Shafi'i that it is to be spent on the caliph after him, because he, upon him be blessings and peace, was entitled to it by virtue of his imamate (leadership), not his prophethood, so that this would be further from the suspicion of a wage for conveying the message. The majority of the Shafi'is hold that what belonged to him, upon him be blessings and peace, from the one-fifth of the *khums* is spent on the public interests of the Muslims, such as the frontier fortifications, the judges of the lands, the scholars occupied with the sciences of the Shari'ah and its instruments, even beginners, the imams and the muezzins, even if they are wealthy, and all others who are occupied, away from their livelihood, with the public interests of the Muslims, because of the general benefit they provide. Added to them are those who are incapable of earning and of receiving, as the ruler decides, considering the abundance and scarcity of wealth. The most important is given priority over the less important, as an obligation. The most important of all is the defense of the frontiers.

The return of his share, upon him be blessings and peace, to the Muslims after his death is indicated by his statement, upon him be blessings and peace, in the sound report: «What belongs to me of what Allah, exalted is He, has granted you is nothing but the *khums*, and the *khums* is returned to you.» It is consistent with spending it on the public interests of the Muslims, just as it is consistent with adding it to the remaining shares so that it is divided among the rest of the categories with them. Its clear meaning is not conceded to be in this and not that.

And there is one share for the near of kin, one share for the orphans, one share for the needy, and one share for the wayfarer. These are the five shares of the *khums*. By "the near of kin" is meant his relatives, Allah bless him and give him peace. What is meant by them is the Banu Hashim and the Banu al-Muttalib, because he, upon him be blessings and peace, placed the share among them, to the exclusion of the Banu Abd Shams, their full brothers, and of his descendants, Uthman, and their paternal half-brother Nawfal. He answered this by his statement, upon him be blessings and peace: «We and the Banu al-Muttalib are one thing,» and he interlaced his fingers [to illustrate]. Al-Bukhari related it. That is, they did not separate from the Banu Hashim in supporting him, upon him be blessings and peace, in the Jahiliyyah or in Islam. Perhaps because of their strong solidarity and their unity, as if they were of one heart, it was said: "to the near of kin" (singular) rather than "to the kinsfolk" (plural).

The Shafi'is said: The wealthy and the poor share in this portion, because of the unrestricted wording of the verse, and because he, upon him be blessings and peace, gave al-Abbas, who was wealthy. It was even said that he had twenty slaves who traded for him. The women also share, because Fatimah and Safiyyah, the paternal aunt of her father, may Allah be pleased with both of them, used to take from it. The male is given preference, as in inheritance, by analogy, since it is an entitlement by paternal kinship; so the male receives the equivalent of two shares of the female. Scholarly and young, and their opposites, are equal in it. If they refuse it, it does not lapse, as with inheritance. A man's being a Hashimi or a Muttalibi is established by proof, and some have stated that along with proof, there must also be *istifadah* (widespread reputation). Ahmad agreed with al-Shafi'i's view. According to Malik, the matter is left to the imam: if he wishes, he divides it among them; if he wishes, he gives some of them and not others; and if he wishes, he gives others, even if his matter is more important than theirs.

Al-Muzani and al-Thawri said: The male and the female are equal, and it is given to the distant and the near among those who have a kinship tie. The wealthy and the poor are equal, because of the unrestricted text, and because a ruling linked to a derived attribute is explained by the root of the derivation. With us, the near of kin is specific to the Banu Hashim and the Banu al-Muttalib, because of the hadith. Yet they do not have a separate independent share, and they are not given in an absolute sense. Rather, their needy, their orphans, and their wayfarers are given, because they are included among the orphans, the needy, and the wayfarers. However, they are given priority over others in these categories, because the three caliphs did not set aside for them a specific share; rather, they divided the *khums* into three shares: one share for the orphans, one for the needy, and one for the wayfarer. Ali, may Allah honor his face, during his caliphate, did not oppose them in this, despite his opposing them in some other matters. [His silence] is to be understood as a return to their opinion, if it is authentically reported from him that he used to say: "The share of the near of kin is as has been related from al-Shafi'i." The benefit of mentioning them, on the view that their entitlement is due to another attribute besides kinship, such as poverty, is to remove the misconception that a poor person among them, for example, does not deserve anything, because it would be from the category of *sadaqah* (charity), which is not lawful for them. Whoever surveys the reports will find much disagreement in them. Among them are reports indicating that the caliphs used to give them shares without restriction. This is the view of the scholars of the Ahl al-Bayt (People of the House). Some of our companions chose that what is mentioned in the verse are the *masarif* (channels of expenditure) of the *khums*, in the sense that each category may be given from it, not that they are the rightful recipients. Thus it is permissible, according to us, to limit the distribution to a single category, such as giving the entire remainder of the *khums* to the wayfarer alone, for example.

The discussion is fully treated in the commentaries on *al-Hidayah*. By "the orphans" is meant those of them who are poor. The Shafi'is said: The orphan is a child who has no father, even if he has a grandfather. Islam is a condition for him, and poverty or indigence, according to the well-known position, because the term "orphan" implies need. The benefit of mentioning them alongside the inclusion of the needy among them is that they are not deprived, lest one suppose that they are not fit for jihad, and that they be singled out for a complete fifth. It includes the child of fornication, but not a foundling (*laqit*), according to the more likely view, because we have not verified the absence of his father. And he is wealthy through his maintenance from the public treasury (*bayt al-mal*). Proof is necessary to establish the orphanhood, Islam, and poverty here. For the needy and the wayfarer, their own statement suffices, even without an oath, even if they are suspected. Yet it appears that a claimant of the loss of property, who has a known customary standing or dependents, is required to produce proof. End of quotation. The condition of poverty for orphans is explicitly stated in most of our books. Let the rest be consulted.

This being so, the remaining four-fifths, according to the statement of the author of *al-Kashf*, who was a Shafi'i, after he chose to read "for the poor" (*lil-fuqara'*) as a substitute for "the near of kin" and what is conjoined to it, because it includes His words, exalted is He: ﴿and those who settled [in the abode] before them﴾ up to His words, glory be to Him: ﴿and those who came after them﴾, according to the meaning that it is for him, upon him be blessings and peace, to benefit people with it as he chooses. He said: It is for the fighters now, according to the more correct view. In Ibn Hajar's *Tuhfah*, it is stated that according to the more apparent view, it is for the paid soldiers (*murtaziqah*), their judges, their imams, their muezzins, and their officials, so long as no voluntary contribution (*tabarru'*) is found. The *murtaziqah* are the soldiers registered in the military register for jihad, because victory is obtained through them after him, upon him be blessings and peace. The *Tuhfah* explicitly states that the majority hold that these four-fifths were for him, upon him be blessings and peace, along with the one-fifth of the *khums*. Thus the total of what he, upon him be blessings and peace, used to take from the *fay'* was twenty-one shares out of twenty-five. Al-Ruyani said that he would spend the twenty shares that were his, upon him be blessings and peace, that is, the four-fifths, on public interests, obligatorily according to one view and recommendedly according to another. Al-Ghazali said: All of the *fay'* belonged to him, upon him be blessings and peace, during his lifetime, and it was only divided into fifths after his death.

Al-Mawardi said: It was for him (ﷺ) at the beginning of his life, and then it was abrogated (*naskh*, abrogation) at its end.

Al-Zamakhshari said: The Exalted's words ﴿what Allah bestowed﴾ and so on are an explanation of the first sentence, meaning His words ﴿And what Allah bestowed upon His Messenger from them﴾. For this reason the conjunction (*'atif*) was not applied to it. In it He explained for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) what he should do with what Allah bestowed upon him, and commanded him to place it where he places the one-fifth (*khums*) of the spoils, divided among the five categories. Its apparent meaning is that the sentence is an explanatory resumption (*isti'naf bayani*), and the question concerned the expenditure of what Allah bestowed upon His Messenger (ﷺ) from the Banu al-Nadir. The first sentence indicated that his command (ﷺ) is delegated to him, and it does not necessarily follow that it must be divided in the manner of spoils over which a substantial battle was fought, and which were taken by force and conquest, as the warriors requested. Rather, the four-fifths of them are for them. And what is placed in the position of the one-fifth of the spoils is the whole, not that its one-fifth is likewise. The remainder, which is four-fifths of it, is for those included in the Exalted's words ﴿And those who had settled [in the city] and [adopted] the faith﴾ up to His words ﴿And those who came after them﴾, as you have heard earlier. And the intended meaning of the people of the towns is the same as the intended meaning of the pronoun in "from them", that is, the Banu al-Nadir. He turned away from the pronoun to that (expression), according to what is in *al-Irshad*, to indicate that what is in ﴿what Allah bestowed﴾ also includes their properties (*'aqarat*).

The author of *al-Kashf* objected to what the apparent meaning suggests, namely that the verse indicates His command to him (ﷺ) to place the whole in the position where he places the one-fifth of the spoils. The import of the verse, with which he supported his position, and he examined the matter closely; so let it be consulted and pondered.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: The people of the towns mentioned in the verse are the people of al-Safra', Yanbu', and Wadi al-Qura, and what is there of the towns of the Arabs called the towns of 'Uraynah. Their ruling differs from the ruling on the properties of the Banu al-Nadir, for all of those belonged to him (ﷺ) exclusively, whereas these he divided like the others. It is also said: What is meant by "what Allah bestowed upon His Messenger" is Khaybar. Half of it was for Allah and His Messenger (ﷺ), and the other half for the Muslims. What was for Allah the Exalted and His Messenger, peace be upon him, from that was al-Katibah, al-Watih, Salalim and Wakhdah. What was for the Muslims was al-Shiqq, which was thirteen shares, and Natah, which was five shares. He (ﷺ) did not distribute anything of Khaybar to any of the Muslims except to those who had witnessed al-Hudaybiyah. He (ﷺ) did not permit anyone who had stayed behind from him when he set out for al-Hudaybiyah to attend Khaybar with him, except Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah

[Page 49]

ibn 'Amr al-Ansari. This is also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas. Some scholars restricted what Allah bestowed to the poll-tax (*jizyah*) and the land-tax (*kharaj*).

It is narrated from al-Zuhri that he said: It has reached me that this is so. You have heard that 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, argued with this verse for leaving the fertile land of Iraq in the hands of its people, and imposed the land-tax and poll-tax upon them, in response to those who requested that it be divided among the warriors along with its non-Arab inhabitants. But that was only because the benefit of what Allah bestowed reached the general body of Muslims in the manner mentioned, without distribution. So understand.

In the repetition of the preposition (*lam*) before "the Messenger" and "the near kindred", along with the conjunction, there is an evident concern (for them). It is said that this contains support for those who hold that their two shares do not lapse. As for the singular form "the near kindred", we have mentioned its reason, which is not far-fetched. And since the wayfarers are in the position of relatives, He said ﴿and the wayfarer﴾ in the singular, just as He said ﴿and to the near kindred﴾. Upon this is the poet's verse:

*O neighbour, we are two strangers here,*
*And every stranger is a kinsman to a stranger.*

﴿So that it does not become⟩ is a rationale for the division. The pronoun in "it becomes" refers to what Allah bestowed, meaning: so that the spoil does not become ﴿a circulating commodity [dawlah]﴾. It is with a *damma* (*dawlah*), and likewise with a *fatha* (*dawlah*), for what circulates for a person of wealth, striving and dominance. Al-Kisa'i and the expert grammarians of Basra said: *al-dawlah* with a *fatha* refers to sovereignty, and with a *damma* refers to wealth, and *al-dawlah* with a *kasra* refers to... Or it is with a *damma* in wealth and with a *fatha* in victory. It is said: and in rank. It is also said: The *damma* form is what is circulated, like *ghurfah* (a scoop), which is a noun for what is scooped, while the *fatha* form is a verbal noun meaning circulation. Al-Raghib, 'Isa ibn 'Umar and many others held that the two have the same meaning. Most of the readers recited with a *damma* on the *dal* and an accusative on the word, with the letter *ya'* below in "yakun", on the basis that the subject of "yakun" is the pronoun and "dawlatan" is the predicate, meaning: so that the spoil does not become a great fortune ﴿among the rich among you﴾, meaning among them alone, multiplying through it. Or: so that it does not become a circulating power and a pre-Islamic dominance among you, for their leaders used to monopolize the spoils and say: "Who is mightier?" It is also said: The meaning is so that it does not become something the wealthy pass among themselves and exchange, so that none of the poor obtains a share of it.

'Abd Allah (ibn Mas'ud) read "takun" with a *ta'* above, on the basis that the pronoun refers to the meaning, since what is intended by it is the wealth. Abu Ja'far and Hisham read likewise, and read "dawlah" in the nominative with a *damma* on the *dal*, on the basis that *kana* is complete and "dawlah" is the subject, meaning: so that a circulation does not occur. 'Ali and al-Sulami also read likewise, and read "dawlatan" in the accusative with a *fatha* on the *dal*, on the basis that *kana* is incomplete, its subject being what you have heard, and "dawlatan" its predicate. A modifier (*mudaf*) must be assumed if it is taken as a verbal noun, unless it is used figuratively and no exaggeration is intended, meaning: so that it does not become something circulating among the rich, which they do not bring out to the poor. The apparent sense of the stated rationale is that poverty is considered in those mentioned, and that His exaltedness is not characterised by it is necessary. Moreover, His mention was, according to the majority, for blessing and not because He has a share. Likewise, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) is too exalted to be called poor. What is famously attributed to him (ﷺ), "Poverty is my pride," has no basis. How could such a thing be imagined, when the whole world is not worth a gnat's wing in the sight of Allah the Exalted, and he (ﷺ) is the most beloved of His creation to Him, to the point that one of the gnostics said: He should not be called an ascetic (*zahid*) (ﷺ), because the ascetic is one who renounces the world, and he (ﷺ) does not turn towards it, let alone seek it, which renunciation necessarily requires. It is also said: If the report were authentic, the meaning of poverty in it would be complete severance from what is other than Allah, the Exalted, and this is not the poverty under discussion. Considering it for those after him poses no problem, to the extent that it may even be evidence for the view that the rich among the near kindred are not given, but only their poor. And if the statement is taken as we have taken it, it suffices for the rationale that those to whom a part of the spoil is given be poor, and it does not follow that everyone who is given a part of it is poor.

[Page 50]

﴿And whatever the Messenger gives you﴾, meaning what he gives you of the spoil, ﴿take it﴾, because it is your right, which Allah has made lawful for you. ﴿And whatever he forbids you﴾, meaning from taking it from him, ﴿abstain﴾ from it. ﴿And fear Allah﴾ in opposing him (ﷺ). ﴿Indeed, Allah is severe in punishment﴾, so He punishes whoever opposes him (ﷺ). Restricting the verse to the spoil specifically is narrated from al-Hasan, and that was due to the contextual indication. In *al-Kashshaf* it is said: The better view is that it is general in everything he (ﷺ) commanded and forbade, and the matter of the spoil falls within the generality. That is because of the generality of the word "whatever" (*ma*). Moreover, the conjunction "and" cannot be taken as a coordinating conjunction, so it is a parenthetical insertion in the manner of a concluding appendage (*i'tiradh 'ala sabil al-tadhyil*). For this reason it is followed by His words ﴿And fear Allah﴾, a generalisation upon a generalisation. It thus encompasses everything that must be guarded against, and what the discourse was originally about enters by primary inclusion, just as it enters the first generality. This was narrated from Ibn Jurayj.

Al-Shaykhan (al-Bukhari and Muslim), Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi and others narrated from Ibn Mas'ud that he said: "Allah has cursed the women who tattoo and those who have themselves tattooed, the women who pluck their facial hair and those who file their teeth for beauty, who alter Allah's creation." This reached a woman from the Banu Asad called Umm Ya'qub, who used to recite the Qur'an. She came to him and said: "It has reached me that you cursed such and such." He said: "Why should I not curse one whom the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) cursed, and who is in the Book of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic?" She said: "I have read what is between the two covers of the Mushaf and have not found it." He said: "If you had read it, you would have found it. Have you not read His words ﴿And whatever the Messenger gives you, take it, and whatever he forbids you, abstain﴾?" She said: "Yes." He said: "Indeed, he (ﷺ) has forbidden this."

It is narrated from al-Shafi'i that he said: "Ask me about whatever you wish, and I will inform you of it from the Book of Allah and the Sunnah of His Prophet (ﷺ)." 'Abd Allah ibn Muhammad ibn Harun said: "What do you say about the muhrim (one in the state of ihram) who kills a wasp?" He said: Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And whatever the Messenger gives you, take it, and whatever he forbids you, abstain﴾.

Sufyan ibn 'Uyaynah narrated to us from 'Abd al-Malik ibn 'Umayr, from Rib'i ibn Khirash, from Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Follow the two after me, Abu Bakr and 'Umar." Sufyan ibn 'Uyaynah narrated to us from Mis'ar ibn Kidam, from Qays ibn Muslim, from Tariq ibn Shihab, from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, that he commanded the killing of the wasp. This is among the strange forms of inference. In it, despite its weaknesses, like the statement of Ibn Mas'ud, is the application of what is in the verse to generality. And from Ibn 'Abbas there is also something indicating this. It is said: The meaning then is: "Whatever the Messenger gives you of the command, hold fast to it, and whatever he forbids you from engaging in, abstain from it." The word "command" (*amr*) may be taken as the singular of "affairs" (*umur*), or as the singular of "commands" (*awamir*), to contrast with his forbidding you. It is said: The first is closer, because one does not say "he gave him the command" meaning "he commanded him" except with strain, as is not hidden. It is deduced from the verse that the obligation of abstention depends upon the establishment of a prohibition, and the absence of a command is not sufficient for it. Thus what he has neither commanded nor forbidden is not obligatory.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 59, verse 8:

﴿For the poor emigrants﴾. Al-Zamakhshari said: It is a substitute (badal, apposition) for His saying, exalted is He, "for the near of kin," and what is conjoined to it. What prevents substitution from "﴿Then to Allah and to the Messenger﴾" and what follows it, although the meaning is for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), is that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, removed His Messenger, upon him be prayer and peace, from the poor in His saying, glorified is He: "﴿and they help Allah and His Messenger﴾." Also, the Messenger of Allah, upon him be prayer and peace, is exalted above being named "the poor." Furthermore, substitution according to the apparent wording goes against what is obligatory in glorifying Allah, Mighty and Majestic. This is like how it is not permissible to describe Him, glorified is He, with a feminine marker for the sake of grammatical gender, because that is a breach of etiquette. End of quotation.

In my view, it is a substitution of the whole for the whole (badal kull min kull), in consideration that the substituted element (al-mubdal minhu) comprises all that was mentioned. The Imam said: It is as if it were said, "I mean by those four these poor emigrants." The substitution from "for the near of kin" and what follows it is based on the view of the Hanafis, that the wealthy among the near of kin are not given, and only the poor are given. As for one who holds, like al-Shafi'i, that their wealthy are given just as their poor are given, he restricts the substitution to the orphans and what follows. It has also been said that this is permissible too, but he holds that the poverty is specified by the spoils of the Banu al-Nadir, for the Prophet, upon him be prayer and peace, did not give any of it to a wealthy person, and the verse was revealed concerning it. But this is a clear strain.

In the Kashshaf, it is said that "for the poor" is not a restriction, but an explanation of the reality of the emigrants' condition and an affirmation of the increased specificity of their claim, as if it were said: "to Allah and to the Messenger and to the emigrants." Ibn 'Atiyya said: "for the poor, etc." is an explanation of His saying, exalted is He: "the orphans and the needy and the wayfarer." The preposition lam (of the genitive) was repeated because what preceded it was governed by it, to clarify that the substitution is from it. It has also been said that the lam is connected to what His saying, exalted is He, indicates: "﴿so that it will not be a perpetual distribution among the rich among you﴾," as if it were said: "But it shall be for the poor emigrants."

If Allah, exalted is He, wills, what has occurred to us regarding this possibility will come later, based on what is understood from the apparent words of Umar ibn al-Khattab, in the presence of a group of the Companions.

﴿Who were expelled from their homes and their wealth﴾: the disbelievers of Makkah compelled them and forced them to leave, so they departed from it. This is a description according to the general case. It has been said that these were a hundred men.

﴿Seeking bounty from Allah and approval﴾: that is, seeking from Him, exalted is He, provision in this world and well-pleasure in the Hereafter. They were first described with what indicates their entitlement to the spoils, namely their expulsion from their homes and wealth. Then this was qualified secondly by what makes their standing great, and it is confirmed by what indicates their complete reliance on Allah and their contentment with what the Sovereign, the All-Knowing, has decreed.

﴿And they help Allah and His Messenger﴾ is conjoined to "seeking," so it is a presumed circumstantial clause (hal muqaddarah), meaning intending to support Allah, exalted is He, and His Messenger, Allah bless him and grant him peace. Or it is a concurrent circumstance, since their departure from among the disbelievers, defying them, emigrating to Madinah, is support, and what support it is!

﴿Those﴾, described with what has been mentioned of the noble qualities, ﴿they are the truthful﴾: that is, the perfect in truthfulness in their claim of faith, since they did what indicates it most strongly, together with their expulsion from their homelands and wealth for its sake, not others who believed in Makkah but did not leave their homes and property, and did not display anything like what was displayed by them, due to some softness toward the polytheists. Thus the restriction is relative. It has been explained otherwise as well.

Some have taken the statement in a general sense, by omitting the object of "truthful," and have relied on this to argue for the validity of the imamate of Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, because these emigrants used to call him "the Caliph of the Messenger of Allah," Allah bless him and grant him peace, and Allah has testified to their truthfulness, so his imamate, may Allah be pleased with him, must be valid and established in reality. This is a weak argument, and the claim that the validity of al-Siddiq's caliphate is established by the consensus (ijma') of the Companions, including Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, does not need such an argument. Attributing taqiyya (precautionary dissimulation) to him by way of agreement, which the Shi'a do not agree to, is not the act of a pious person, like the claim of coercion. Rather, it is also unnecessary for other reasons.

[Page 51]

﴿Those who had settled in the abode and in faith﴾. Most scholars hold that this is conjoined (ma'tuf) to "the Emigrants" (al-Muhajirun), and that by them is meant the Helpers (al-Ansar). Tabawwu' means to settle in a place, and from it comes al-mabaa'a, meaning a dwelling. Its attribution to "the abode" (al-dar), meaning Medina, is clear. As for its attribution to faith, it is by way of treating faith as a settled and established home, in the manner of the metaphor (isti'ara) that is implicit (makniyya) and imaginative (takhyiliyya). The definite article in "the abode" (al-dar) serves to draw attention to it, as though it were the abode truly deserving of the name "abode," namely the one that Allah the Exalted prepared for them, so that their settling in it would be a praise of them.

Others have said: the expression is of the type of "I fed her straw and cold water," meaning: they settled in the abode and sincerely held to faith. It has also been said that tabawwu' is a metonymy (majaz mursal) for lazum (adhering to), and its necessary meaning is intended, so it is as though it were said: "they adhered to the abode and to faith." It has also been said, as an explanation of this, that the "al-" in "al-dar" is for a known reference (al-'ahd), and that what is meant is the abode of emigration (dar al-hijra), which serves the function of a possessive construction (idafa). In "wal-iman" there is the omission of a modified noun (mudaf), meaning "and the abode of faith." So it is as though it were said: "they settled in the abode of emigration and the abode of faith," with the two abodes being understood as Medina. The conjunction is like your saying: "I saw the rain and the lion," while you mean Zayd. The defect of this is not hidden, for it contains much artificiality and forced interpretation. It has also been said that "faith" is a metaphor for Medina, the place where something appears being named after it, for emphasis; but this is, as you see, weak. It has also been said that the "wa" is for accompaniment (ma'iyya), and that what is meant is "they settled in the abode together with their faith," meaning "they settled in it as believers." This also is nothing of worth. The best of these views is the one we mentioned first. Some have mentioned that "al-dar" is a proper name by predominance for Medina, like "Medina" itself, and that it is one of its names, among them Taiba, Taba, Yathrib, and Jabira, and others besides.

Al-Zubayr ibn Bakkar narrated from Zayd ibn Aslam a hadith traced to the Prophet (ﷺ) that indicates this. ﴿From before them﴾, meaning before the Emigrants. The prepositional phrase is connected to "tabawwu'u," and the sentence implies an omitted modifier, meaning "from before their emigration." Thus the furthest that is required is that the Helpers preceded the Emigrants in faith by their emigration; it does not follow from this that their faith preceded the faith of the Emigrants, so that one could say the matter is the reverse. It has been permitted that no modifier be supposed, and it is said: the intended meaning is not that the Helpers preceded them in the basic faith itself, but rather that they preceded them in establishing themselves in it, since they were not disputed in it because of what they had shown.

It has been said: the sentence is one of inversion and reordering, and the meaning is "they settled in the abode before them and in faith," so it conveys only that they preceded them in settling in the abode. This goes against the apparent sense. Moreover, such a view is not acceptable unless it includes a subtle point, and that point is not apparent here. It has also been said: there is no need for any of what has been mentioned, and the most that the verse indicates is the precedence of the whole of the Helpers' settling and faith over the settling and faith of the Emigrants; and the precedence of the whole is sufficed by the precedence of one of its parts, which here is the settling in the abode. This has been challenged by denying that it suffices; and even if it were granted, it would be proper to say: the settling of the Emigrants and their faith precede the settling of the Helpers and their faith, because the faith of the Emigrants precedes [the faith of the Helpers].

﴿They love those who emigrated to them﴾: this is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) from the relative pronoun (al-mawsul). It has also been said that it is a resumptive new sentence (isti'naf). It has been said that the sentence is a metonymy (kinaya) for their comforting the Emigrants and for their not finding it burdensome or resentful of them when they were in need of them. It has also been said that it is according to its apparent meaning, namely: they love the one who emigrated to them, from the standpoint of his emigration to them, because of their love for faith.

﴿And they do not find in their breasts﴾, meaning: they do not know in themselves.

﴿Any need﴾, meaning a request of one in need of something. ﴿Of what they were given﴾, meaning of what the Emigrants were given of the spoils (fay') and other things. The essence of this is that their souls did not follow what was given to the Emigrants, nor did they aspire to any part of it that they might need. So "wijdan" (finding) is a cognitive perception, and its being "in the breast" is by way of metaphor. "Haja" (need) is in the sense of "that which one needs," and this is a common usage: one says "take from him your need" and "he gave him from his wealth his need." The "min" (of) is partitive, but it has been permitted that it be explicative, with an omitted modifier, which is "a request." In this there is a great benefit, as though they had never conceived of that, nor had it crossed their minds that it was something they needed, so that their souls would aspire to it.

It is possible that the meaning is: they do not find in themselves that which would produce need, such as resentment, anger, envy, or covetousness on account of what the Emigrants were given. The word "need" is then a metaphor for what results from it. It has been said that this is a metonymy for what has been mentioned, because it does not separate from need, so the name of the necessary concomitant is applied to that which entails it. But what came before is more appropriate. The statement of some of them, "What trace of need?", is a statement of meaning, not of i'rab (grammatical analysis). The "min" in His words ﴿of what they were given﴾ is causal.

﴿And they prefer﴾, meaning they give precedence to the Emigrants ﴿over themselves﴾ in everything of the good things. So much so that whoever had two wives would withdraw from one of them and marry her to one of them. It is permitted that the object of "yu'thiruna" not be restricted to the Emigrants alone. Al-Bukhari, Muslim, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i, and others narrated from Abu Hurayra who said: "A man came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, hunger has afflicted me.'
