He sent to his wives, but found nothing with them. Then he said, peace and blessings be upon him: 'Will not a man host this man tonight? May Allah have mercy on him.' A man from the Helpers said, and in another narration Abu Talha said: 'I, O Messenger of Allah.' So he took him to his household and said to his wife: 'Honour the guest of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).' She said: 'By Allah, I have nothing but the food of the children.' He said: 'When the children want their dinner, put them to sleep, and come, extinguish the lamp, and we shall go hungry tonight for the guest of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).' She did so. Then the guest went in the morning to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he said: 'Allah was amazed tonight at so-and-so and so-and-so,' and Allah the Exalted revealed concerning them: ﴿and they prefer﴾." Etc.

Al-Hakim, who graded it sound, and Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman narrated from Ibn Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: "A sheep's head was sent as a gift to a man among the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he said: 'My brother so-and-so and his dependants are in greater need of this than we are.' So he sent it to him, and that one sent it to another, until it passed around among the people of seven houses, until it returned to the first. Then there was revealed: ﴿They prefer over themselves, even though they themselves were in need﴾." Here "khasasa" means need arising from the gaps of the house, which are the openings and spaces left between its beams. The sentence is in the position of a circumstantial clause, and the reason for this has been explained many times before.

﴿And whoever is protected from the stinginess of his soul﴾. Shuhh is baseness, and it is that the soul be tight-fisted and greedy to withhold, as the poet said:

"He exercises a soul between his two sides, tight-fisted; when he resolves upon good, it says to him: 'Gently!'"

It is attributed to "the soul" because it is an innate disposition in it. As for bukhl (miserliness), it is the withholding itself. Al-Raghib said: shuhh is miserliness together with greed, and that applies to what has become a habit. Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from al-Hasan that he said: bukhl is that a person is miserly with what is in his hand, while shuhh is that he is greedy over what is in the hands of people.

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Shayba, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman, al-Hakim, who graded it sound, and a group narrated from Ibn Mas'ud that a man said to him: "I fear that I have perished." He said: "And what is that?" He said: "I heard Allah the Exalted say: ﴿And whoever is protected from the stinginess of his soul﴾, and I am a stingy man, nothing of mine ever comes out." Ibn Mas'ud said to him: "That is not shuhh, but it is bukhl, and there is no good in bukhl. The shuhh that Allah the Exalted mentioned is that you consume the property of your brother unjustly." Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, that he said: "Shuhh is not that a man withholds his property, rather that is bukhl. Shuhh is only that a man's eye covets what is not his." I have not seen any of the lexicographers give any of these explanations for shuhh. Perhaps the intended meaning is that it is extreme miserliness, to the point that the one characterized by it is miserly with another's wealth, meaning he does not wish the generosity of another with it, his soul contracts from it, and he strives that it not happen; or to the point that greed carries him to consume his brother's property unjustly, that his eye covets what is not his and his soul does not permit that it belong to another. So reflect.

Abu Haywa and Ibn Abi 'Abla read "wa-man yuwaq" with a doubled qaf. Ibn Umar and Ibn Abi 'Abla read "shuhha" with a kasra on the shin, and a fath (a) vowel is also attested for it, and the meaning of all is one. The meaning of the verse: "whoever is protected," by Allah the Exalted's granting of success and assistance, "from the stinginess of his soul," so that he opposes it in what predominates over it of love of wealth and hatred of spending. ﴿Those are the successful﴾, meaning those who attain every desired thing and are saved from every disliked thing. The conditional sentence is a fine concluding statement and a praise of the Helpers with what is the ultimate end of their being included initially in the address. The shift to the singular first and the plural afterward is in observance of the wording and meaning of "man" and an allusion to how few are those characterized by this in actuality, and to their greatness in meaning:

"People are a thousand, of whom one is like a thousand; and one, if the matter is grave, is like a thousand."

It is understood from the verse that stinginess is greatly condemned, and many reports have been transmitted condemning it. al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi, Abu Ya'la, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Anas, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ): "Nothing has ever destroyed Islam as stinginess has destroyed it." Ibn Abi Shayba, al-Nasa'i, al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman, and al-Hakim, who graded it sound, narrated from Abu Hurayra, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ): "The dust of the way of Allah and the smoke of the fire of Hell do not gather in the belly of a servant ever; and faith and stinginess do not gather in the heart of a servant ever." Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, who said it is gharib (strange), al-Bukhari in al-Adab, and others narrated from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ): "Two qualities do not gather in the belly of a Muslim: miserliness and bad character." Ibn Abi al-Dunya, Ibn 'Adi, al-Hakim, and al-Khatib narrated from Anas who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Allah the Exalted created the Garden of Eden and planted its trees with His own hand. Then He said to it: 'Speak!' It said: 'The believers have succeeded.' Then Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: 'By My might and My majesty, no miser shall be my neighbour in you.' Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited: ﴿And whoever is protected from the stinginess of his soul, those are the successful﴾."

Ahmad, al-Bukhari in al-Adab, Muslim, and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah that the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "Beware of injustice, for injustice is darkness on the Day of Resurrection. And beware of stinginess, for stinginess has destroyed those who were before you; it drove them to shed their blood and to make lawful what was forbidden to them." And other reports besides these.

However, it should be known that protection from stinginess is not conditioned upon a person being generous with everything. Abd ibn Humayd, Abu Ya'la, al-Tabarani, and al-Diya' narrated from Majma' ibn Yahya, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever pays the zakat, hosts the guest, and gives in times of calamity, is free from stinginess."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated something close to this from Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, and likewise Ibn Jarir and al-Bayhaqi from Anas. Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from 'Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, who said: "Whoever pays the zakat of his wealth has been protected from the stinginess of his soul."

The commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on Surah 59, verse 10:

And His saying, ﴿And those who came after them﴾, is also, according to most scholars, coordinated with (ʿatf) the Emigrants (al-muhajirun). By "these" is meant, it is said: those who emigrated when Islam had become strong. Thus "coming" is literal, namely their coming to Medina. The pronoun in ﴿after them﴾ refers to the first Emigrants. It is also said that they are the believers after both groups until the Day of Resurrection. In that case "coming" is either coming into existence or coming to faith, and the pronoun in ﴿after them﴾ refers to both groups, the Emigrants and the Helpers (al-Ansar). This is what the statement of ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, indicates, and the statements of many of the early generations (al-salaf) are explicit in it. So the verse encompasses all the believers. The clause of His saying, ﴿they say﴾ and so on, is a circumstantial clause (hal). It is also said to be a resumptive statement (istiʾnaf). ﴿Our Lord, forgive us and our brothers﴾, that is, in religion, which is more honoured and more noble in their view than lineage, ﴿who preceded us in faith﴾. They described them thus, acknowledging their virtue. ﴿And do not place in our hearts any rancour (ghill)﴾, that is, hatred. It was also read as ghamran. ﴿towards those who believe﴾, without restriction. ﴿Our Lord, You are indeed Compassionate, Merciful﴾, that is, exceedingly abundant in tenderness and mercy. Therefore You are worthy to answer our supplication. In the verse there is an exhortation to pray for the Companions and to purify the hearts from hatred of any of them. ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and a group related from ʿAʾisha, may Allah be pleased with her, that she said: "They were commanded to seek forgiveness for the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ, but they reviled them. Then she recited this verse: ﴿And those who came after them﴾ and so on."

Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with them both, that he heard a man disparaging some of the Emigrants, so he called him [Page 55] and recited to him ﴿for the poor Emigrants﴾ (59:8) and so on. Then he said: "These are the Emigrants. Are you one of them?" He said: "No." Then he recited to him ﴿and those who settled in the abode and in the faith﴾ (59:9) and so on. Then he said: "These are the Helpers. Are you one of them?" He said: "No." Then he recited to him ﴿and those who came after them﴾ (59:10) and so on. Then he said: "Are you one of these?" He said: "I hope so." He said: "No, by Allah, one who reviles these is not among these."

In another narration, Ibn ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, was informed that a man had spoken ill of ʿUthman, may Allah be pleased with him, so he summoned him, recited the verses to him, and said to him what he said. Imam Malik said: "Whoever has an evil statement or hatred towards any of the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them all, has no share in the fayʾ (spoils), taking this verse as evidence." The verse also indicates the condemnation of rancour towards any of the believers. In a hadith related by al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi and al-Nasaʾi from Anas, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Prophet ﷺ said: "Within three days there will appear to you now a man from the people of Paradise." Then a man from the Helpers appeared, and ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAs stayed with him three nights, seeking to observe his condition. He did not see from him much action, so he informed him of the matter. He said to him: "It is nothing but what you have seen, except that I do not find in my heart any rancour towards any Muslim, nor do I envy him for any good that Allah, may He be exalted, has given him." ʿAbd Allah said to him: "This is what has reached you, and this is what we are unable to match." In another narration, he said: "If the world were mine and it were taken from me, I would not grieve over it; and if I were given it, I would not rejoice in it. I spend the night and there is no rancour in my heart towards anyone." ʿAbd Allah said: "But I stand in prayer at night and fast by day. If a sheep were given to me I would rejoice in it, and if it were lost I would grieve over it. By Allah, Allah has indeed favoured you over us with a clear favour."

This is the end of the matter. Some have held that His saying, ﴿And those who settled﴾ and so on, is a new subject (mubtadaʾ), and the clause ﴿they love﴾ and so on is its predicate (khabar). The discourse is a resumptive statement brought to praise the Helpers. It is permitted that this be coordinated with ﴿those﴾ (ulaʾika), in which case it indicates that the Helpers share with the Emigrants in truthfulness. The clause ﴿they love﴾ and so on is either a confirming resumptive statement of their truthfulness or a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in ﴿settled﴾. And some have held that His saying, ﴿And those who came﴾ and so on, is a subject, and the clause ﴿they say﴾ and so on is its predicate. The clause is coordinated with the preceding clause, brought to praise these people for their love of those who preceded them among the believers, and their observance of the rights of brotherhood in religion and of precedence in faith, just as the preceding clause it is coordinated with is brought to praise the Helpers.

It has been argued for the view that ﴿those who settled﴾ is not coordinated with ﴿the Emigrants﴾ by what is related: that the Prophet, may the prayers and peace be upon him, divided the wealth of the Banu al-Nadir among the Emigrants and gave the Helpers nothing except three men, as mentioned earlier. He, may the prayers and peace be upon him, said to them: "If you wish, I will divide [the property] among the Emigrants from your wealth and your homes, and you may share with them in this booty; and if you wish, your homes and your wealth will be yours, and nothing of the booty will be divided among you." They said: "Rather, we will divide for them, that is, for the Emigrants, from our wealth and our homes, and we will prefer them with the booty, and we will not share in it with them." So the verse was revealed: ﴿And those who settled the abode and the faith﴾ to its end. Some who hold the view of coordination say that His saying, ﴿And those who settled﴾ and so on, is an explanation of the ruling concerning the four-fifths (al-akhmas al-arbaʿa), in the sense that it is for him, may the prayers and peace be upon him, to spend them on people as he chooses, and that the Helpers are one of the recipients (masarif). However, the Prophet, may Allah exalt him and grant him peace, chose that their giving should be on the condition he stated to them, may the prayers and peace be upon him, and they chose what they chose out of preference. That does not remove them from being recipients. Indeed, in His saying, ﴿and they prefer [others] over themselves﴾ there is an allusion to this. Moreover, among the reports there is what is more authentic and more explicit in indicating their coordination with what precedes, and that they are given from the fayʾ. Likewise is the coordination of ﴿those who came after them﴾. For al-Bukhari, Muslim, Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasaʾi, Ibn Hibban and others related from Malik ibn Aws ibn al-Hadathan, in a lengthy hadith, that ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, said, namely in his judgment between ʿAli, may Allah honour his face, and his uncle al-ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him, concerning Fadak, which ʿUmar had given to the two of them, taking from them a covenant of Allah that they would act regarding it as the Messenger of Allah, may the prayers and peace be upon him, had acted regarding it, but they disputed: "Allah, may He be exalted, said: ﴿And what Allah restored to His Messenger from them, you did not spur for it any horse or camel, but Allah gives authority to His messengers over whomever He wills, and Allah is over all things competent﴾ (59:6). So it was specifically for the Messenger of Allah, may Allah exalt him and grant him peace. Then He, glorified be He, said: ﴿What Allah restored to His Messenger from the people of the towns, it is for Allah and for the Messenger and for the near of kin﴾ (59:7) to the end of the verse. Then, by Allah, he did not give it to these alone, until He, exalted be He, said: ﴿For the poor Emigrants who were expelled from their homes and their wealth, seeking bounty from Allah and approval, and supporting Allah and His Messenger; those are the truthful﴾ (59:8). Then, by Allah, he did not make it for these alone, until He, glorified be He, said: ﴿And those who came after them say: Our Lord, forgive us﴾ to His saying: ﴿Merciful﴾ (59:10). So he divided it in this manner among those whom He mentioned. And if I live, the shepherd in Sanaʾa will surely come to his share, even if his blood and his face are at [a distance]." The apparent meaning of this report requires that the Emigrants have a share distinct from the previously mentioned shares. Therefore ﴿for the poor﴾ cannot be a substitute (badal) for ﴿for the near of kin﴾ and what follows it, nor for what follows it without it. Likewise is the apparent meaning of what is in the codex of ʿAbd Allah and Zayd ibn Thabit, as related by Ibn al-Anbari in the book of codices (al-Masahif) from al-Aʿmash: "What Allah restored to His Messenger from the people of the towns, it is for Allah and for the Messenger and for the near of kin, and the orphans, the needy, the wayfarer, and the Emigrants in the way of Allah." According to this, the substitution apparently requires that the orphans be Emigrants who were expelled from their homes and wealth, and the rest of the attributes; and in the truthfulness of that concerning them there is doubt. Likewise it requires that the wayfarer be so as well, and in this too there is a degree of remoteness, as is not hidden. Perhaps he considered its connection to a verb that is omitted, and the clause is an explanatory resumption (istiʾnaf bayani). That is because they knew that the fifth (khums) is spent on those included in His saying: ﴿So for Allah and for the Messenger and for the near of kin, the orphans, the needy, and the wayfarer﴾ (8:41). When that was mentioned, it occurred to their minds that those mentioned are the recipients of the fifth, and they did not know the recipients of the remaining four-fifths. So it is as if they said: "For whom then are the remaining four-fifths, or for whom is the remainder?" It was said: "The remaining four-fifths, or the remainder, is ﴿for the poor Emigrants﴾" and so on to the end. I have not seen anyone who addressed this, so reflect. And Allah, exalted be He, is the Guide to the best paths.

﴿Have you not seen those who hypocritically said﴾: this is a narration of the false statements and corrupt conduct that passed between the disbelievers and the hypocrites, and an expression of wonder at them after the narration of the praiseworthy conditions of the believers in their various ranks. The address is to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), or to anyone fit to be addressed. The verse, as Ibn Ishaq, Ibn al-Mundhir and Abu Nu'aym narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, concerns a group from Banu 'Awf, among them 'Abdullah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul, Wadi'ah ibn Malik, Suwayd and Dais, who sent to Banu al-Nadir the message contained in the quoted statements introduced by the words of the Exalted: ﴿They say﴾, and so on.

Al-Suddi said: some people from Banu Qurayzah and al-Nadir embraced Islam, and among them were hypocrites, so they sent to Banu al-Nadir what Allah the Exalted has related. The one relied upon is the first report. The words of the Glorified, ﴿They say﴾, form a resumptive clause (isti'naf) explaining what is being wondered at. The use of the present tense (mudari') indicates the continuity of their saying, or the bringing to mind of its image. The lam in the words of the Almighty and Majestic, ﴿to their brothers who disbelieved among the People of the Book﴾, is the lam of communication (li-l-tabligh). The meaning of their "brotherhood" is brotherhood in religion and in adherence to the same view, or friendship. The plural of akh (brother) is commonly used, when meaning the aforementioned sense, as ikhwan, and when meaning brotherhood by lineage, as ikhwah; the opposite of this is rare. The lam in the words of the Exalted, ﴿If you are expelled﴾, is the lam that prepares for an oath (muwatti'ah lil-qasam), and the words of the Glorified, ﴿we will certainly go out with you﴾, are the answer to the oath. That is: "By Allah, if you are expelled from your homes by force, we will certainly go out from our homes with you, and we will absolutely accompany you wherever you go."

﴿And we will not obey anyone against you﴾, meaning concerning your affair, ﴿who would prevent us from going out with you﴾. This is to exclude the possibility that they would promise the Jews to go out only on condition that they be prevented from doing so, ﴿ever﴾, even if time passes. It was also said: "we will not obey [them] in fighting you or forsaking you." Al-Irshad says: this is not the case, because the supposition of fighting is still awaited, and because their promise to them on that supposition is not merely a lack of obedience to those who call them to fight them, but rather their support against them, as his saying the Exalted clearly indicates: ﴿And if you are fought, we will surely help you﴾, that is, "we will surely aid you against your enemy." Moreover, calling them to forsake the Jews is something that could not issue from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and the believers, so that they would claim the non-obedience of the hypocrites in it; for if it had been so, it would have been at the moment of their preparedness to support them and manifest their disbelief. There is no doubt that what the Messenger (ﷺ) would do at that moment is kill them, not call them to abandon supporting them. As for going out with them, it is not at this level of manifesting disbelief, because it is possible that they would claim their going out with them was due to the worldly friendship between them, not for agreement in religion. This has been disputed. The answer to "in" (in) is omitted; ﴿we will surely help you﴾ is the answer to an omitted oath placed before the conditional "in", and the same is said of what follows, according to the well-known rule concerning when an oath precedes a condition.

﴿And Allah bears witness that they are indeed liars﴾ in their promises, which were emphasized with oaths.

[Page 57]

The Almighty's statement: ﴿Even if they are expelled, they will not go out with them﴾ to the end. It is a denial of each of their claims in detail, after the general denial of all of them. ﴿And even if they are fought, they will not help them﴾. The matter turned out to be as stated, and the report of their failure to keep their promise was said by some to be a report of the unseen (al-ikhbar bil-ghayb), which is one of the proofs of prophethood and one of the aspects of inimitability (wujuh al-i'jaz). This rests on the view that the surah was revealed before the battle of the Banu al-Nadir, whereas the words of the People of Hadith (Ahl al-Hadith) and of the biographers (al-siyar, the accounts of the Prophet's life and campaigns) indicate otherwise, as has been said.

Some of the eminent scholars said: The Almighty's statement, "They say: If you are expelled, we will certainly go out with you," and so on, is of the category of reporting the unseen, based on what is narrated: that Abdullah ibn Ubayy secretly sent word to them, "Do not leave," and Allah the Exalted informed His Messenger (ﷺ) of what he had secretly sent. ﴿And if they help them﴾ is by way of supposition and assumption, ﴿they will surely turn their backs﴾, that is, the hypocrites, ﴿in flight﴾, ﴿then they will not be helped﴾ afterwards, meaning Allah the Exalted will destroy them, and their hypocrisy will not benefit them because their disbelief has become manifest. Or ﴿they will surely turn their backs﴾ refers to the Jews who were supposed to support the hypocrites, and they will be routed, and the support of the hypocrites will not benefit them. It has also been said that the subject pronoun in ﴿they helped them﴾ refers to the Jews and the object pronoun to the hypocrites, meaning: if the Jews help the hypocrites, the Jews will turn their backs. But this is not valid. It seems that the one who proposed this was prompted by the wish to avoid the apparent contradiction between ﴿they will not help them﴾ and ﴿if they help them﴾ according to the earlier interpretation; we have already indicated how this is resolved without any need for this explanation, the state of which is not hidden.

﴿Indeed, you are more fearsome﴾, i.e., more feared (*marhubiyyah*). On this reading, ﴿*rahbah*﴾ is a *masdar* (verbal noun) of the passive form (*al-mabni lil-maf'ul*), because those addressed, who are the believers, are feared by them, not fearers. ﴿In their breasts, [more than] Allah﴾: i.e., their dread of you in secret is greater than what they display to you of their dread of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. They used to show you intense dread of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. It is also possible to mean that they fear you in their breasts more than they fear Allah the Exalted, and because of their extreme courage and boldness they did not display that. It has been said that ﴿in their breasts﴾, according to the first interpretation, is hyperbole and vivid depiction, in the manner of "I saw it with my own eyes." ﴿That﴾: i.e., what has been mentioned, namely that you are more feared in their breasts than Allah the Exalted, ﴿is because they﴾: by reason that they ﴿are a people who do not comprehend﴾ anything, until they know the greatness of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and so fear Him with the fear due to Him, glorified and exalted is He. The intended people here are the Jews. It has been said that they are the hypocrites, and it has been said that they are both groups.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 59, verse 14:

﴿They will not fight you﴾
Page 58

That is, the Jews and the hypocrites. It is also said: the Jews, meaning: they are not capable of fighting you ﴿all together﴾, that is, gathered and united in a single place of the places (of battle), ﴿except within fortified towns﴾, protected by trenches (durub) and ditches (khandaq) and the like, ﴿or from behind walls﴾, which they use as cover, rather than coming out to you and confronting you in open combat, because of God Most High casting terror into their hearts and their greater fear of you.

Abu Raja', al-Hasan and Ibn Thabbab read "judr" (جُدْرٍ) with a sukun on the dal for lightness; it is also transmitted from Ibn Kathir, 'Asim and al-A'mash. Abu 'Amr and Ibn Kathir, in the well-known transmission, and many of the Meccan readers read "jidar" (جِدارٍ) with a kasra on the jim and an alif after the dal, which is the singular of judur (جُدُرٍ), with the intention being the genus; or what is meant by it is the wall (sur) that comprises the walls and enclosures.

A group of the Meccan readers and Harun, from Ibn Kathir, read "jadr" (جَدْرٍ) with a fatha on the jim and a sukun on the dal. The author of al-Lawami' said: it is the wall (jidar) in the dialect of Yemen. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: its meaning is the base of a building, such as a foundation, and other things. Then he said: it may be that it is from judur al-nakhl (the trunks/bases of the palm trees), that is, from behind their palm groves, since these are among the things one shields oneself with at the time of lining up for battle.

﴿Their might among themselves is severe﴾. This is a resumptive statement (isti'naf) brought to clarify that what has been mentioned of their fear is not due to weakness and cowardice within themselves; for their might, when they fight one another, is severe. Their weakness and cowardice relate only to you, through what God Most High has cast into their hearts of terror.

﴿You think them united﴾, that is, gathered together, bound by affection and unity. ﴿But their hearts are scattered﴾: the plural of shatit (شَتِيتٍ), meaning dispersed, with no affection between them. That is, there is enmity and hostility among them, so they do not support one another in the full sense of support, and they do not shoot from one bow. This is an encouragement to the believers and a strengthening of their hearts for fighting them.

Mubashshir ibn 'Ubayd read "shatan" (شَتًى) with tanwin, taking the alif to be the alif of ilhaq (extension). And 'Abd Allah read "wa-qulubuhum ashuntu" (وقُلُوبُهم أشَتُّ), meaning more or greater in dispersal.

﴿That is because they﴾, that is, the aforementioned scattering of their hearts is due to the fact that they are ﴿a people who do not understand﴾ anything, until they know the ways of harmony and the causes of agreement. It is also said: ﴿they do not understand﴾ that the scattering of hearts weakens their inherent strength which is established in them by nature, and helps to destroy and ruin them. But this is not the point.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 59, verse 15:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Like those before them﴾ is the predicate of an omitted subject, its estimated form being "their likeness" (mithluhum), meaning the likeness of those mentioned among the Jews, the Banu al-Nadir; or [the likeness of] them and of the hypocrites, like the people of Badr, as Mujahid said; or like the Banu Qaynuqa', as Ibn 'Abbas said. They were a tribe of Jews who lived around Medina. The Prophet (ﷺ) fought them on a Saturday, twenty months after the Hijra, in Shawwal, before the battle of the Banu al-Nadir, which took place in the spring of the fourth year, and he (ﷺ) expelled them to Adhruat, as detailed in the books of biography (siyar).

It has also been said: that is, the likeness of these hypocrites is like the likeness of the hypocrites of past nations. ﴿Shortly﴾ is an adverbial of time governing His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿they tasted the evil consequence of their affair﴾, meaning they tasted the bad outcome of their disbelief in a time close to their disobedience; that is, their punishment was not delayed, and they were punished in this world immediately after their disobedience.

It has also been said: ﴿shortly﴾ is in the accusative governed by "like" (mithl), the estimated meaning being "like the occurrence of the likeness of those..." This was objected to: the apparent sense is that the sentence intends an omitted noun whose governing effect is actual on the adverbial, but since it was omitted, the noun it was attached to governs it by standing in its place. It is not hidden that the meaning does not accord with this, because the intent is to liken one likeness to another, that is, the strange attribute of these people to the strange attribute of those before them, not to liken the likeness to an occurrence. It was answered that the construction is an idafa of attribute to its qualified noun, so the comparison returns to likening one likeness to another; as if it were said: "Their likeness is like the likeness of those before them, which occurred shortly." In this there is weakness: that estimate is awkward, and what was mentioned does not remove the awkwardness. The view that an omitted noun is also estimated on the side of the subject, namely "the occurrence of their likeness is like the occurrence of the likeness of those before them shortly," so that the occurrence of a likeness is compared to the occurrence of a likeness, is a forced reading that should not be adopted in eloquent speech.

It has also been said: the governing element is the comparison itself, that is, they resemble them in a short time. It has also been said: it is attached to the particle "ka" (like), because it indicates occurrence. Both views, as you see, are weak. It is not far-fetched for it to be attached to what the relative clause is attached to, namely "from before them," meaning those who were before them in a short time; this conveys that their precedence was a close precedence, and it follows from this that what was done to them, which is the likeness, was close. This is the focal point of the meaning, and it carries a rebuke to them: they had a precedent in the people of Badr or the Banu Qaynuqa', so the traces of what befell them have not faded, and this holds on the estimate of occurrence and the like. The clause ﴿they tasted﴾ explains the likeness and has no place in i'rab. ﴿Shortly﴾ is definitely attached to what follows, on the assumption that by "those before them" is meant the hypocrites of past nations, so reflect on this. ﴿And for them﴾ in the Hereafter ﴿is a painful punishment﴾ whose extent cannot be measured. This clause is said to be coordinated with the preceding clause, even though one is verbal and the other nominal. It is also said to be a presumed circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in ﴿they tasted﴾, and whichever it is, it falls within the scope of the likeness. It is also said to be coordinated with the clause "their likeness is like the likeness of those before them," and its remoteness is not hidden.

Al-Alusi's commentary on surah 59, verse 16:

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿like the Shaytan (Satan)﴾. Many scholars have taken it as the predicate (khabar) of an omitted subject (mubtada'), so that the meaning is: "Their likeness is like the likeness of the Shaytan," with the pronoun in "their likeness" referring here to the hypocrites (al-munafiqin), while in what preceded it refers to the Banu al-Nadir. Others said: the pronoun in "their likeness," assumed in both places, refers to both groups. Some verifying scholars (muhaqqiqin) took it as a second predicate of the omitted subject in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿like the likeness of those﴾, with the pronoun there referring to both groups, except that the first likeness is specific to the Banu al-Nadir and the second is specific to the hypocrites. Each of the two predicates was attributed to that assumed subject, which is added to the pronoun of both, without specifying to which it is attributed by name, relying on the confidence that the listener will assign each to what is fitting and similar to it, as if it were said: "The likeness of those who disbelieved among the People of the Book, in the descent of punishment upon them, is like the likeness of those before them, and the likeness of the hypocrites in their inciting them to fight, as was related about them, is like the likeness of the Shaytan ﴿when he said to man: Disbelieve﴾, that is, he incited him to disbelief with the incitement of one who commands another to what he is commanded to do; so it is a figure of speech and a metaphor. ﴿Then when he disbelieved, he said: Indeed I am free of you; indeed I fear Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾, he disowned him out of fear that he would share in the punishment, and that did not benefit him, as He, Exalted is He, said:

﴿So the outcome of both of them will be that they are in the Fire, abiding therein﴾ forever and ever. ﴿And that is the recompense of the wrongdoers﴾, i.e., abiding in the Fire, ﴿the recompense of the wrongdoers﴾ in general, not only of those mentioned specifically. The majority of scholars hold that what is meant by "the devil" and "the human being" is the category (jins), so the disavowal will take place on the Day of Resurrection. This is the most consistent with the apparent meaning of His words: ﴿Indeed, I fear﴾ etc.

Some have held that what is meant by "the devil" is Iblis, and by "the human being" Abu Jahl, may the curse of God be upon them both. He said to him on the day of Badr: ﴿No one among the people can overcome you today, and I am your protector﴾, until they fell into what they fell into, and then he said: ﴿Indeed, I am free of you. Indeed, I see what you do not see. Indeed, I fear God﴾ ... the verse. In this verse, together with what has preceded from Mujahid, there is a subtle point: when He first likened the state of the hypocrites' brethren from among the People of the Book to the state of the people of Badr, He here likened the state of the hypocrites to the state of the devil in the story of the people of Badr. The meaning of ﴿Disbelieve﴾, when the human being is specified as Abu Jahl, is: "Persist in disbelief," according to some. Al-Khafaji said: there is no need to interpret it in this way, because it is a parable (tamthil).

Ahmad in az-Zuhd, al-Bukhari in his Tarikh, al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman, al-Hakim, who declared it sound, and others related from Ali, may Allah honor his face, that a man was worshipping in his hermitage (sawma'a), and that a woman had brothers. Something befell her, so they brought her to him, and his soul adorned her to him, so he had relations with her and she became pregnant. Then the devil came to him and said: "Kill her, for if they discover you, you will be disgraced." So he killed her and buried her. Then they came to him, seized him and took him away. While they were walking, the devil came to him and said: "I am the one who adorned this for you. Prostrate to me one prostration and I will save you." So he prostrated to him. That is, then
(page 60)
he disowned him and said to him what he said. This is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿like the devil when he says to the human being, "Disbelieve"﴾ ... the verse. This man was Barsisa the monk. His story has been related in a more detailed form than what has been mentioned, and it is well known in the stories of the prophets. In al-Bahr it is said that the devil's saying ﴿Indeed, I fear God﴾ was a show (riya'), and fear does not prevent him from an evil into which he draws the son of Adam. It was also read: "Anna bari'un" (I am free). Al-Hasan, Amr ibn Ubayd and Sulaym ibn Arqam read ﴿فَكانَ عاقِبَتُهُما﴾ with the nominative (raf'), taking it as the subject of kana, and ﴿أنَّهُما إلَخْ﴾ as the predicate in the sense of a verbal noun (masdar), in reverse of the reading of the majority.

Abdullah, Zayd ibn Ali, al-A'mash and Ibn Abi Abla read ﴿خالِدانِ﴾ with the alif, taking it as the predicate of inna. ﴿وفِي النّارِ﴾ is connected to it, and it was fronted for restriction (ikhtisas). ﴿وفِيها﴾ is an emphasis for it and a repetition with its pronoun. It is also permitted that ﴿فِي النّارِ﴾ is the predicate of inna, and ﴿خالِدانِ﴾ a second predicate. In the reading of the majority, it is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in the prepositional phrase.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 59, verse 18:

﴿O you who have believed, fear Allah﴾ in everything you do and everything you leave undone. ﴿And let a soul look to what it has put forward for tomorrow﴾, i.e., what deeds it has sent ahead for the Day of Resurrection. He expressed it this way because the Day of Resurrection is near, as tomorrow is near to today, or because the worldly life is like a day and the Hereafter is its tomorrow, in which there will be states different from the previous states. The indefinite form of "tomorrow" (ghad) is for its magnification and awe, as if it were said: "a tomorrow whose reality is not known because of its immense greatness." As for the indefinite form of "soul" (nafs), it is for the independence of the individual souls that look, as if it were said: "let one soul look into this." This contains a great exhortation to reflection and a rebuke for neglecting it, and [it indicates] that heedlessness has become widespread among all, so that none has been spared from it. From this it becomes clear, as in al-Kashshaf, that taking it as being of the same kind as the words of the Exalted, ﴿a soul will know what it has brought forward﴾ (al-Takwir: 14), does not fit the context. That is, it is like what is in the hadith: "The people are like a hundred camels, among which you will not find a riding camel." For although the command to look is general, those who actually obey and look are fewer than the few, and the purpose of the minimizing is exactly this, because the one commanded does not look unless he obeys. Ibn 'Atiyya permitted that "tomorrow" be understood as the Day of Death, but this is not so. Abu Haywah and Yahya ibn al-Harith read "wa-litanzura" with a kasra on the lam, and this is narrated from Hafs from 'Asim. Al-Hasan read it with a kasra on the lam and a fatha on the ra', making it the lam of kay (purpose), so the meaning would be: "and in order that a soul may look at what it has put forward for tomorrow, we were commanded to be mindful of God." ﴿And fear Allah﴾ is a repetition for emphasis (ta'kid, reinforcement), or the first [fear of Allah] refers to the performance of obligations, as indicated by what follows of the command to act, and this [second] refers to abandoning the forbidden acts, as indicated by the warning in His words, glorified is He: ﴿Indeed, Allah is Acquainted with what you do﴾, i.e., of sins. This second view is more preferable, because of the superiority of establishing new meaning (ta'sis) over emphasis. The occurrence of the two commands unrestricted indicates a grandeur that is not hidden. It was said that mindfulness of Allah includes abandoning what is sinful, and there is no proper basis for the distribution [of the two meanings]. The context is one of concern for its matter, so emphasis is more fitting and stronger. In this there is an evident objection, for how is it not so, when what is understood from "what you have put forward" is the deeds of goodness? Thus it has been said. Perhaps the one who holds the view of emphasis says: the words of the Exalted, ﴿Indeed, Allah is Acquainted﴾ and so on, include both promise and warning and generalize "what you have put forward" as well. Perhaps, despite this, you lean toward establishment (ta'sis).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 59, verse 19:

﴿And do not be like those who forgot Allah﴾, i.e., they forgot His rights, exalted is His majesty, and they did not measure Allah with His true measure, nor did they observe the obligations of His command, glorified is He, and His prohibitions, mighty and majestic is He, with their due observance. ﴿So He caused them to forget themselves﴾: Allah, exalted is He, as a consequence of that, ﴿caused them to forget themselves﴾, i.e., He made them forgetful of them, glorified is He, so that they did not strive for what would benefit them and did not do what would save them. Or, He, majestic is His majesty, showed them on the Day of Resurrection, of the terrors of what caused them to forget themselves, i.e., He showed them a dreadful matter and a painful punishment. The forgetting of the self is a real matter. It has been said: it is of what cannot occur, because knowledge of it is by presence (ḥuḍūrī). But this is open to question, even though Ibn Sina (Avicenna) and his followers stated it explicitly. ﴿Those are the defiantly disobedient﴾, the perfect ones in defiant disobedience.

Abu Haywa read ﴿wa-lā yakūnū﴾ (and let them not be) with the third-person plural (yāʾ al-ghayba), by way of iltifat (shift of grammatical person). Ibn 'Atiyya said: it is a metonymy (kināya) for the very intended meaning, which is the category (al-jins).

[Page 61]

﴿Not equal are the companions of the Fire﴾: those who forgot God, exalted is He, and so deserved abiding forever in the Fire. ﴿And the companions of the Garden﴾: those who were mindful of God, and so deserved abiding forever in the Garden. Perhaps the mention of the companions of the Fire first is to signal from the outset that the deficiency indicated by the non-equality lies on their side, not on the side of their counterparts. The concept of non-equality between two things that differ in excess and deficiency, although it may be considered in terms of the excess of the one who has more, is more readily understood in terms of the deficiency of the one who has less. Consistent with this is the saying of God, exalted is He: ﴿Are the blind and the seeing equal? Or are the darknesses and the light equal?﴾ [al-Ra'd: 16], and other examples.

Perhaps the mention of the superior first in God's saying ﴿Are those who know equal to those who do not know?﴾ [al-Zumar: 9] is because its attribute is a disposition (malakah) for the attribute of the inferior, while its privation (i'dam) is preceded by its dispositions. By non-equality is meant non-equality in the otherworldly conditions, as indicated by the expression of the two groups as "companionship of the Fire" and "companionship of the Garden." Likewise God's saying ﴿The companions of the Garden are the ones who triumph﴾ is a resumptive clause (istinaf) explaining the manner of the non-equality between them: that is, they are the ones who triumph in the Hereafter, attaining every desired thing and being saved from every disliked thing. The verse is an admonition to people and an indication that, due to their extreme heedlessness, their scant reflection on the outcome, and their eagerness to prefer the immediate life and to follow fleeting desires, they behave as though they do not know the difference between the Garden and the Fire, nor the great distance between their respective companions, nor that triumph is with the companions of the Garden. It is therefore their right to know this and to be alerted to it. This is like saying to one who has disobeyed his father: "He is your father," treating him as one who does not know him, so that you remind him of the right of fatherhood, which calls for dutifulness and tenderness.

From what has been mentioned it becomes clear how weak is the argument of the followers of al-Shafi'i, may God be pleased with him, from this verse that a Muslim is not to be killed for a disbeliever, and that disbelievers do not own the property of Muslims by conquest. They defend themselves by saying: since God, exalted and majestic is He, urged piety in deed and in abstention, and warned against heedlessness, which is its utter opposite, by mentioning its ultimate end, namely forgetting God, exalted is He, as an intensifier of rebuke, He then followed it by saying that the people of piety and the people of this heedlessness are not equal in anything at all. He described them as the companions of the Garden and the companions of the Fire for added depiction and clarification. Thus the context requires difference in the rulings of the two abodes, although the primary intended purpose is their difference in the abode which is the place of recompense. You know that the demonstration that the context requires this is in response to the statement of the followers of Abu Hanifa: the context requires specification, otherwise the Shafi'is say that generality is the implication of negating equality in the lexical sense, because the negation enters upon the concept of equality, so it must be negated in all respects; for if it existed in one respect, its concept would not be negated, and this contradicts the apparent meaning of the wording. The Hanafis' statement is that equality in general is broader than equality in every respect, equality in some respects, and equality in one respect only, and the negation has entered upon the broader equality, so it does not indicate either of the two specific kinds.

The summary of this is that the general does not indicate the specific within it. This holds for affirmation, which is accepted, but for negation it is disputed. Do you not see that one who says "I have not seen an animal," having in fact seen a human, for example, is deemed a liar? The full treatment of this is in the books of legal theory (usul al-fiqh). The fair judgment is that the intended meaning here is the negation of equality in the otherworldly matters, which is very evident, so the verse should not be used as evidence for what has been mentioned.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 59, verse 21:

﴿Had We sent down this Qur'an﴾ — the Qur'an being of great majesty, embracing the various kinds of awe-inspiring calamities — ﴿upon a mountain﴾ — one of the mountains, or a great mountain — ﴿you would have seen it﴾ — despite it being a byword for hardness and for being unaffected by whatever strikes it — ﴿humbled, split apart out of fear of God﴾, i.e., cracked open from it.

Abu Talha read ﴿mutasaddi'an﴾ (muṣaddaʿan) with the assimilation of the tā' into the ṣād. This is an image and an imaginative depiction (tamthil wa-takhyil) of the exalted status of the Qur'an and the strength of the effect of the admonitions and warnings it contains. The purpose is to rebuke the human being for the hardness of his heart and his lack of humility when reciting the Qur'an and reflecting upon its awe-inspiring content, for he is the one for whom, if it were sent down upon a mountain endowed with intellect, it would have humbled itself and split apart. That this is an image is indicated by God's words:

﴿And these are the parables We present to the people, that perhaps they will reflect﴾ — for the reference in it is to His words ﴿Had We sent down﴾ etc., and to similar examples. The statement is thus understood as though such things had occurred, or the intended meaning is "those and their like," and parables (amthal) are, for the most part, imagined depictions (tamthilat mutakhayyilah).

He is Allah, there is no deity except Him. [He is] alone, glorified is He. ﴿The Knower of the unseen﴾, which is that which no created being's knowledge or perception has ever reached, and this is the absolute unseen. ﴿And the witnessed﴾, which is that which a created being witnesses.

Al-Raghib (al-Raghib al-Isfahani) said: al-shuhud and al-shahadah mean presence together with observation, either by sight or by insight. Presence may be considered alone, but al-shuhud (as presence without observation) is more appropriate, and al-shahadah (as presence with observation) is more appropriate. Taking al-ghayb (the unseen) to mean the absolute is what comes first to mind, and the alif-lam in it is for comprehensiveness (istighraq), since there is no indication that it refers to a specific known thing. The context of praise requires this, together with His saying: ﴿Knower of the unseen things﴾ [al-Ma'idah 109, 116; al-Tawbah 78; Saba' 48]. So it includes every unseen thing, whether necessary, possible, existent, non-existent, or impossible, which no created being's knowledge has reached. Al-ghayb is also applied to that which the knowledge of a specific created being has not reached, and this is al-ghayb al-mudaf (the relative unseen), meaning the unseen in relation to that created being. It is said that this is what the jurists mean in their saying: "One who claims knowledge of the unseen is a disbeliever." And this may be from the realm of the witnessed, as is not hidden.

Mentioning al-shahadah, although if every unseen thing is known to Him, then every witnessed thing is known to Him, glorified is He, by a fortiori reasoning, in line with His saying, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿He leaves nothing small or great unrecorded except that He has counted it﴾ [al-Kahf 49]. It is also said: al-ghayb is that which the senses do not reach, whether it is non-existent or existent but not perceptible, and al-shahadah is that which is reached by perception through the senses.

Imam Abu Ja'far, may Allah be pleased with him, said: al-ghayb is what has not yet come to be, and al-shahadah is what has come to be. Al-Hasan said: al-ghayb is the secret, and al-shahadah is the open. It is said: the first is this world with what is in it, and the second is the Hereafter with what is in it. It is said: the first is the pure substances (al-jawahir al-mujarradah) and their states, and the second is the bodies and physical forms and their accidents. In this there is a strong disagreement about the existence of the pure substances, and most of the Salaf (the early generations, the pious predecessors) held that they do not exist.

The unseen is mentioned first because knowledge of it is like evidence for knowledge of the witnessed. It is also said: it is because of its precedence over the witnessed, for every witnessed thing was once unseen, and nothing emerged except from the treasuries of the unseen. The proponent of the last opinion says: the unseen is mentioned first because of its precedence in existence and the attachment of eternal knowledge to it. The verse has been cited as evidence that He, exalted is He, knows all knowable things, and its reasoning is what we have pointed out. It is said that it also contains another proof of this, because it indicates that there is no worshipped one except Him, and this necessarily entails that He, glorified is He, is the Creator of everything by choice, as is the reality in fact. Creation by choice is impossible without knowledge. For this reason it is said that using this verse for this matter is better than using His saying: ﴿And Allah is Knower of all things﴾ [al-Baqarah 282; al-Nisa' 176; al-Nur 35, 64; al-Hujurat 16; al-Taghabun 11].

﴿He is the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful﴾, with a mercy befitting His essence, glorified is He. As for ta'wil (figurative interpretation), although distinguished scholars of the Maturidiyyah and the Ash'ariyyah have mentioned it, the Salafi (one who follows the way of the early pious generations) has no need for it, as has been verified in al-Tamyiz and elsewhere.

[Page 63]

﴿He is Allah, other than whom there is no deity﴾. It is repeated to show the utmost concern with the matter of tawhid (affirmation of God's oneness).

﴿al-Malik﴾ (the King): the One who disposes of affairs through command and prohibition; or the Owner of all things, who has disposal over them; or the One who grants honour to whom He wills and humiliates whom He wills, and for whom humiliation is impossible; or the One who appoints and dismisses, and for whom appointment or dismissal cannot be conceived; or the One who alone possesses might and sovereignty; or the Possessor of kingship, while kingdom is His creation; or the Able. These are opinions related by al-Amidi, and the last was related from al-Qadi Abu Bakr.

﴿al-Quddus﴾ (the Holy): the One who is most absolutely free from whatever would imply deficiency; or the One who has perfection in every attribute specific to Him; or the One who cannot be limited or conceived. Abu al-Sammal and Abu Dinar al-A'rabi read «al-Qaddus» with a fatha on the qaf. This is a dialectal variant of it, but it is rare. For they have said: the pattern fu'ul with a damma is common, whereas with a fatha it occurs among names, like sammur, tannur, and habbud, which is the name of a mountain in al-Yamamah. As for its occurrence among attributes, it is extremely rare, and among these is subbuh with a fatha on the sin.

﴿as-Salam﴾ (the Source of Peace): the One who is free from every deficiency and blemish. It is a verbal noun (masdar) used as a descriptive for the sake of intensification (mubalaghah, emphasis). According to al-Jubba'i, it means the One from whom safety is hoped for. It has also been said: that is, the One who greets His allies with peace, so they are safe from every fearful thing.

﴿al-Mu'min﴾ (the Giver of Security): it has been said: the One who confirms Himself and His messengers, peace be upon them, in what they have conveyed from Him, glory be to Him, either by speech or by creating a miracle. Or: the One who grants His servants security from the greatest terror, or who secures them from it, either by creating tranquillity in their hearts or by informing them that there is no fear for them. It has also been said: the One who secures creation from His own injustice. Tha'lab said: the One who confirms the believers in their having believed. Al-Nahhas said: in their testimony over people on the Day of Resurrection. It has also been said: the One who is secure from cessation, since that is impossible for Him, glory be to Him. Other opinions have also been given. Imam Abu Ja'far Muhammad ibn Ali ibn al-Husayn, may Allah be pleased with them, read — or it was Abu Ja'far al-Madani — «al-Mu'man» with a fatha on the mim, by elision and transitivity (hadhf wa iisal), as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And Musa chose his people﴾ [al-A'raf: 155], meaning al-Mu'man bihi (the One in whom one is secure, or the One given security).

Abu Hatim said: it is not permissible to apply this to Allah, the Exalted, because it gives the impression of what is not fitting for Him, glory be to Him, since the absolute mu'man is one who was fearful and was made secure by someone else. It is said in reply: if this is a recitation, even an irregular one (shadhdh), this objection would not hold, because recitation is not a matter of opinion.

﴿al-Muhaymin﴾ (the Guardian): the Watchful, the Preserver of everything. It is of the pattern mufay'il, derived from amn (security), with its hamza changed to a haa'. Many have taken this view. Its verification, as in al-Kashf, is that aymin is of the pattern fay'al, an intensive form of amman (he made secure) for the sake of added structure. When you say, for example, "the shepherd secured the flock from the wolf," this indicates the complete preservation and watch over them. Thus Allah has secured everything other than Himself, glory be to Him, over His creation and His dominion, owing to the comprehensiveness of His knowledge and the perfection of His power, mighty and majestic is He. Then the mere meaning of the verb was used in the sense of "watchful over" and "preserving over" something, with the object mentioned without an intermediary, for the sake of intensifying complete preservation, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿and a guardian over it﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 48]. To take it from this root is better than taking it from amanah (trustworthiness), since "one who is trusted with something" is a guardian of it, but that does not express intensification or the comprehensiveness of knowledge and power.

In al-Sihah, he took it as an active participle from amanahu al-khawf (he secured him from fear), according to the original root, so the original hamza was changed to a ya' because of the dislike of two hamzas coming together, and the first was changed to a haa', as in haraqa al-ma' (he poured out the water). The saying of people in iyyaka, "hayyaka," is also similar, as if He, by His preservation of created beings, made them secure. The preposition "ala" (over), as in "muhayminan 'alayhi," is for the sake of implying the meaning of supervision and similar notions. You know that the derivation as you heard first is more indicative, and departure from analogy in it is less. The apparent meaning of al-Kashf's statement is that it is not at all a diminutive.

Al-Mubarrad said: it is a diminutive. He was judged to be in error in this, for it is not permissible to diminutivize the names of Allah, mighty and majestic is He.

﴿al-Aziz﴾ (the Mighty): the Dominant. It has been said: the One who has no equal. It has been said: the One who punishes whom He wills. It has been said: the One upon whom rests the reward of those who act. It has been said: the One whose station cannot be lowered. Other opinions have also been given.

﴿al-Jabbar﴾ (the Compeller): the One who compelled His creation to what He willed and forced them to it. It is said of His act: ajbar. Forms of intensification are derived from non-triliteral roots, but rarely. It has also been said that it is from jabarahu, meaning "reformed him": from it comes "I set the bone and it was set," so He is the One who set the affairs of His creation, that is, reformed them. It has also been said: He is the Unassailable, whom none can reach. It is said of a palm tree when it grows tall and hands cannot reach it: jabbarah. It has also been said: He is the One whose action is not contested, who is not required to give a reason, and whose power is not restricted.

Ibn Abbas said: He is the Great. Other opinions have also been given.

﴿al-Mutakabbir﴾ (the Supremely Great): the One who is complete in majesty and greatness, since He, glory be to Him, is free of the burden (taklif) indicated by the form of the word. This is traced back to its implication that an action arising from careful perfection is stronger and more eloquent. Or: the One who is exalted above everything that would imply need or deficiency.

﴿Glory be to Allah above what they associate with Him﴾: this is the declaring of Allah, exalted is He, free from what they associate with Him, glory be to Him, or free from their associating anything with Him, mighty and majestic is He, following the enumeration of His attributes, exalted is He, none of which can be shared by anything else in any way at all.

[Page 64]

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 59, verse 24:

﴿He is Allah, the Creator (al-Khaliq)﴾ who determines things according to the requirement of wisdom; or the Originator of things without any prior material or pattern to imitate. Creation (khalq) is interpreted as bringing a thing into existence. ﴿al-Bari'﴾ (the Evolver) is the One who brings them into being free from disparity in what their wisdom and natural constitution require; and it is said: the One who distinguishes some of them from others by their differing forms. ﴿al-Musawwir﴾ (the Fashioner) is the One who brings into being their forms and modes as He wills.

Al-Raghib said: The form (suwrah) is that by which essences are imprinted and distinguished from others. It is of two kinds: the perceptible, which both the common and the elite perceive, indeed humans and many animals perceive it, like the visible form of a horse; and the intelligible, which only the elite perceive, not the common people, like the form peculiar to humans in intellect, reflection, and the meanings by which one thing is distinguished from another. To both forms He alluded with His saying, glorified is He: ﴿We created you, then We fashioned you﴾ [al-A'raf: 11], along with other verses. End of quotation, so do not be heedless.

Ali (may Allah ennoble his face), Hatib ibn Abi Balta'ah, al-Hasan and Ibn al-Sumayfa' read «al-Musawwara» with a fatha on the waw and in the accusative, as an object of al-Bari', and the intended meaning is the category of the fashioned things. It is also reported from Ali (may Allah ennoble his face) that he read it with a fatha on the waw and a kasra on the ra', making the active participle an annexed noun to its object, like "al-darib al-ghulam" (the one who strikes the boy). In al-Khaniyyah it is stated that reciting «al-Musawwara» with a fatha on the waw here invalidates the prayer. Perhaps he meant if one applies it to Allah, glorified is He, in that case; otherwise, claiming invalidation after what you have heard is open to question.

﴿To Him belong the Most Beautiful Names﴾ which indicate beautiful meanings. ﴿Whatever is in the heavens and the earth glorifies Him﴾ among existing things, by the tongue of state, on account of the wisdoms and benefits they contain, which the scope of expression cannot contain; or by the tongue of speech which each of them has been given, according to what befits it, as many of the knowers have said, and the discussion of this has already preceded. ﴿And He is the Almighty, the All-Wise﴾, who combines all perfections entirely, for they, despite their multiplicity and diversity, return to the perfection of power, indicated by ﴿al-Aziz﴾ (the Almighty) based on interpreting it as the Overpowering, and to the perfection of knowledge, indicated by ﴿al-Hakim﴾ (the All-Wise) based on interpreting it as the Doer according to the requirement of wisdom. In this there is an allusion to adornment after purification, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿There is nothing like Him, and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing﴾ [al-Shura: 11]. So reflect, and do not be heedless.

For these verses there is great merit, as many reports indicate. Imam Ahmad, al-Darimi, al-Tirmidhi, who graded it sound (hasan), al-Tabarani, Ibn al-Darис, and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman narrated from Ma'qil ibn Yasar, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "Whoever says, when he enters the morning, three times: 'I seek refuge in Allah, the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing, from the accursed Satan,' then recites the last three verses of Surah al-Hashr, Allah appoints over him seventy thousand angels who send blessings upon him until evening; and if he dies that day, he dies a martyr. And whoever says it when he enters the evening has the same station."

Al-Daylami narrated from Ibn Abbas, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ): "The Greatest Name of Allah is in the six verses at the end of Surah al-Hashr."

Abu 'Ali 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Muhammad al-Naysaburi narrated in his Fawa'id from Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyyah that al-Bara' ibn 'Azib said to Ali ibn Abi Talib (may Allah ennoble his face): "I ask you by Allah, to single me out with the best of what the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him) singled you out with, of what Gabriel brought, of what the Most Merciful, Mighty and Majestic, sent." He said: "O Bara', when you want to call upon Allah by His Greatest Name, recite ten verses from the beginning of al-Hadid and the end of al-Hashr, then say: 'O You who are such, and there is nothing such besides You, I ask You to do for me such and such.' By Allah, O Bara', if you were to invoke against me, I would be swallowed up by the earth."

Al-Daylami narrated "from Ali (may Allah ennoble his face) and Ibn Mas'ud (may Allah be pleased with him), traced to the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him), that he said concerning His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Had We sent down this Qur'an upon a mountain﴾ to the end of the surah: it is a remedy for headache."

Al-Khatib al-Baghdadi narrated in his History: Abu 'Ubayd al-Hafiz informed us, Abu al-Tayyib Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yusuf ibn Ja'far al-Muqri' al-Baghdadi, known as Ghulam Ibn Shanabudh, informed us, Idris ibn 'Abd al-Karim al-Haddad informed us, who said: "I recited to Khalaf, and when I reached this verse, ﴿Had We sent down this Qur'an upon a mountain﴾, he said: 'Place your hand on your head, for I recited to Hamzah, and when he reached this verse he said: place your hand on your head, for I recited to al-A'mash, and when he reached this verse he said: place your hand on your head, for I recited to Yahya ibn Wthab, and when he reached this verse he said: place your hand on your head, for I recited to 'Alqamah and al-Aswad, and when they reached this verse they said: place your hand on your head, for we recited to 'Abd Allah (may Allah be pleased with him), and when we reached this verse he said: place your hands on your heads, for I recited to the Prophet (peace be upon him), and when I reached this verse he said to me: place your hand on your head, for when Gabriel (peace be upon him) descended with it to me, he said: place your hand on your head, for it is a cure for every disease except al-Sam, and al-Sam is death.'" And other narrations to this effect. And Allah knows best.
